REPORT
CHAPTER - I
BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
1.0. The Union Ministry of Law and Justice comprises of three Departments, namely, the
Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and Department of Justice and through the
said Departments, the Ministry assists in the process of orderly change directed towards realization
of the objectives set out in the Constitution.
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
1.1. As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department of
Legal Affairs renders advice to various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal
matters and carry out the litigation work in various Courts, including the Supreme Court. Besides
this, it is also concerned with the appointment of Law Officers, namely the Attorney General for
India, the Solicitor General of India and the Additional Solicitor Generals of India, assists in
entering into treaties with foreign countries in matters of civil law on behalf of the President of
India. It is also the nodal authority in respect of Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange, the
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and National Tax Tribunal.
1.2. The Department of Legal Affairs has a two tier set up, namely, the Main Secretariat at New
Delhi and the Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Bangalore. The nature of duties
discharged by the Main Secretariat and Branch Secretariats can be broadly classified into two areas
- Advice work and Litigation work. Advice caters to Central Government Departments/Offices at
Centre and in States/UTs and Litigation work relates to Central Administration Tribunal (CAT), High
Courts and Supreme Court.
1.3. The following are the organizations/institutions, which come under the overall supervision
of Department of Legal Affairs and get Grant-in-aid for their research works:-
(a) Law Commission of India: -  The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory
body, constituted by the Government once in three years. The Commission was first
constituted in 1955. It consists of a Chairman, three full-time Members, one
Member-Secretary and three or more part-time Members, depending upon the nature
of work. Law Commission Reports are considered to be primary source of law
reforms for Parliament, as well as the judiciary.
(b) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT): -  Section 252 of the Income Tax Act,
1961 provides that the Central Government shall constitute an Appellate Tribunal
consisting of as many Judicial Members and Accountant Members as it thinks fit,
to exercise the powers and discharge the functions conferred on the Appellate
Tribunal by said Act.
(c) Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange (ATFE): -  The Appellate Tribunal of
Foreign Exchange was established on 1
st June 2000 vide Government of India

2
Notification No. S.O. 531 (E), dated 1.6.2000 issued under section 18 of the
Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA),
(d) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860 is engaged in research in the field of law.
(e) International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution (ICADR):- The
International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution was registered under the
Societies Registration Act, 1860 on 31
st May 1995. It is an autonomous organisation
working under the aegis of the Department.
(f) Bar Council of India (BCI): - The Bar Council of India is a statutory body
constituted under the Advocates Act 1961, which has been empowered among other
things to lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers,
maintain and improve the standard of legal education in the country.
(g) Institute of Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies (ICPS):-  The Institute of
Constitutional and Parliamentary Studies is a private body engaged in research in the
field of constitutional and parliamentary studies and came into existence in 1965.
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT
1.4. The Legislative Department acts mainly as a service provider in so far as the legislative
business of the Union Government is concerned. The Department is entrusted with legislative
matters and is responsible for drafting of all Government Bills and Ordinances and scrutiny and
vetting of subordinate legislations sponsored by various Union Ministries/ Departments. Rendering
assistance to Parliament and Joint/Standing Committees in respect to Bills before its enactment. It
is also administratively concerned with certain matters such as the Code of Civil Procedure,
Limitation and Arbitration, Contracts, Personal Laws, Evidence and Transfer of Property. There are
over hundred Central Acts falling under these subjects.
1.5. The Department has two wings under it mainly:-
(i) Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research : With a view to increase the
availability of trained legislative draftsmen in the country, the Institute of Legislative
Drafting and Research was established as a Wing of the Legislative Department,
Ministry of Law and Justice in January, 1989.
(ii) Official Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan : The Official Languages
Wing is a successor Organisation of the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission
under the Legislative Department. It has been entrusted with the preparation and
publication of a standard legal terminology for use in all Official Languages;
authoritative texts in Hindi of all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations
promulgated by the President, all rules, regulations and orders made by the Central
Government under any Central Act and authoritative texts of all Central Acts and
Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the President in the respective Official
Languages of the States and to arrange for the translation of all Acts passed and
Ordinances promulgated in any State into Hindi, if the texts of such Acts or
Ordinances are in a language other than Hindi.

3
1.6 Election Commission of India:  Legislative Department is also administratively concerned
with the Election Commission of India and Election laws connected with election to Parliament and
State Legislatures and to the offices of the President and the Vice-President. There is a separate
Demand No.55 for the Election Commission of India.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
1.7. The duties of the Department of Justice, as per the Government of India (Allocation of
Business) Rules, 1961, include the administration of justice and the processing of appointment of
judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial
Officers in Union Territories, creation of All India Judicial Service and extension/exclusion of the
jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory.
1.8. The following institutions/autonomous bodies/policy initiatives come directly under the
overall supervision of Department of Justice:
(a) Supreme Court of India:-  There is a separate demand No.57 (Appropriation)
pertaining to the Supreme Court of India. The expenditure to be incurred on the
Supreme Court of India is ‘Charged’
 expenditure .
(b) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA):-  The National Legal Services
Authority has been constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to
monitor and evaluate implementation of legal aid programmes and to lay down
policies and principles for making legal services available under the Act. The NALSA
issues guidelines for the State Legal Services Authorities to implement the legal aid
programmes which are in turn discharged through the following services:-
(i) Free Legal Services: It includes court fees, process fee and all charges
payable or incurred in connection with any legal proceedings, providing
Advocate in legal proceedings, etc.
(ii) Lok Adalats: -  Lok Adalat is a forum where the disputes/cases pending in
the court of law or at pre-litigation stage are settled/compromised amicably.
The Lok Adalat has been given statutory status under the Legal Services
Authorities Act, 1987.
(c) Family Courts/Special Courts :- The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a
view to providing for establishment of Family Courts, to promote conciliation and
secure speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage, family affairs and related
matters. In accordance with the provisions of section 3 of the Act, the State/UT
Governments can establish Family Courts in the areas comprising districts, towns,
city in the States having population of ten lakhs. Even the States/UTs are competent
to establish such court in those areas with the State/UT having a population less
than ten lakhs in consultation with the concerned High Court.
(d) National Judicial Academy :- The National Judicial Academy was registered as a
Society under the Societies Registration Act and came into existence with effect
from 17
th August, 1993. The affairs of the Academy are managed by a Governing

4
Council, which is chaired by the Chief Justice of India. The registered office of the
Academy is in Supreme Court Building at New Delhi and another office was
established in August, 2000 at Bhopal. The main objectives of the Academy are to
impart training to the Judicial Officers of the States/Union territories and to study
the court management and administration of justice in States and Union territories.
(e) Centrally Sponsored Scheme: The Government is implementing a Centrally
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for development of infrastructure facilities for judiciary
since 1993-94. The scheme covers construction of court buildings and residential
accommodation of judicial officers/judges covering only Subordinate courts. Under
the Scheme, funds are provided to the States to augment their capacities for
infrastructure development of the District and Subordinate Courts. The modified
CSS is to be implemented in a Mission Mode approach over the years 2011-16 under
the National Mission.
(f) National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms:  Set up for five years
in 2011, and became fully functional with effect from the financial year 2012-13.
The twin goals of the Mission include increasing access by reducing delays and
arrears in the system and enhancing accountability at all levels through structural
changes and setting performance standards and facilitating enhancement of
capacities for achieving such performance standards. The four schemes proposed to
be pursued under the Mission are as under;
(a) Scheme for Computerization of the District and Subordinate Courts / E-
Courts.
(b) Access to Justice - Government of India.
(c) Strengthening of Access to Justice in India (SAJI (EAP).
(d) Action Research and Studies on Judicial Reforms.
(g)   Access to Justice- Externally Aided Project (UNDP assisted)
The Project started in 2009 with support under the United Nations Development
Programme (UNDP). The Project is being implemented in 7 States (Bihar,
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) and
aims to strengthen access to justice for the marginalized - particularly women,
scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and minorities - by supporting strategies and
initiatives that seek to address the barriers they face.
 (h) Access to Justice- North-East and Jammu and Kashmir (Government of India
Project)
The Project started in 2012 and covers the 12
th Five year Plan period (2012-2017)
to venture in those regions of the Country which have so far been under-represented
and unheard in the arena and discourses of Access to Justice. The project aims to
make Justice accessible to the marginalised sections of the society. The project aims
to train lawyers, law students and customary judicial officers to raise awareness

5
among people about their legal rights. It is hoped that the project will be a milestone
in establishing a model of access to justice in remote areas of North East Region
and Jammu & Kashmir.
(i)    Computerization of District and Subordinate Courts E-courts Mission Mode
Project Phase-I & II :- This is a scheme proposed in the 12
th Plan with components
such as computerisation of 1000 new Courts, use of solar energy under e-Courts
Project, computerisation of the Public Prosecutors Office, videoconferencing facility
for jails, enhancement of ICT infrastructure of courts, digitization of old case
records, computerisation of Judicial libraries, up-gradation of application software,
SMS based services, Touch Screen Kiosks with a provision of ` 1280 crore which
would spread over a period of five years.
(j) Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 :-
The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for
the establishment of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root level for the purpose of
providing speedy and inexpensive access to justice to the citizens at their door steps.
The Central Government would meet 50% of the recurring expenses to be incurred
on the setting up of these courts in the first three years subject to a ceiling of
` 3.20 lakhs per annum.
(k) The Fourteenth Finance Commission  has recommended ` 9,749 crore to the
Department of Justice for pendency reduction by establishing additional courts, Fast
Track Courts, establishment of Family Courts, redesigning existing courts to make
them litigant-friendly, augmenting technical support for e-courts, scanning and
digitalization, Access to justice- legal aid, Lok Adalats, ADR, Training and capacity
building of judges, public prosecutors, mediators and lawyers and establishing state
judicial academies for Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura.

CHAPTER – II
AN OVERVIEW OF THE BUDGET ALLOCATIONS DURING 2016-17
2.0. The total budgetary allocations for the Ministry of Law and Justice for the year 2015-16
are shown under the following three Demands: -
(i) Demand No. 55  pertains to the Election Commission, which is under the
administrative control of the Legislative Department;
(ii) Demand No. 56  is the consolidated Budget Estimates pertaining to the Department
of Legal Affairs, the Legislative Department and the Department of Justice under the
Ministry of Law and Justice;
(iii) Demand No. 57  pertains to the Supreme Court of India, which is under the

EVM & VOTER VERIFIABLE PAPER AUDIT TRAIL SYSTEM (VVPAT) 
3.12. V oter-verified paper audit trail (VVPAT) is a method of providing feedback to voters using
a ballot less voting system. Under VVPAT, a printer-like apparatus is linked to Electronic V oting
Machine (EVM). When a vote is cast, a receipt is generated showing the serial number, name and
symbol of the candidate. It confirms the vote and the voter can verify the details.
3.13. The Commission submitted that EVMs are produced by two public sector units, i.e. BEL
and ECIL. These are the only two units which are authorized to produce it and have the expertise
and all the securities relating to EVMs. So, EVMs and VVPATs are the two machines which are

15
to be procured in order to phase out the pre-2006 machines and to meet the demands for the Lok
Sabha elections. The Commission has informed that VVPAT was used in select polling stations in
8 States (Bihar, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Uttar Pardesh and West Bengal) and
the Commission is overall satisfied with the VVPAT in these States. As against the demand for
` 1800 crores in BE (2016-17), an allocation of ` 1700 crores has been allocated for the purpose
to the Legislative Department, which is the administrative Department for the procurement of
EVMs and VVPATs.
3.14.  While making his submission before the Committee the Director-General, Election
Commission of India stated that the:-
….our total requirement of EVMs for 2019 General Elections is 16,35,000 VVP ATs,
16,35,000 Control Units and 22,37,000 Ballot Units. From the numbers available, the
balance which has to be procured is, 16,15,000 VVP ATs, 9,30,000 Control Units and
13,95,000 Ballot Units. So, these have to be procured before December, 2018 for the
elections to be conducted in 2019. Keeping the production capacity of the two companies,
i.e., BEL and ECIL, we have projected the requirement over the next three years, which
comes close to 
` 5,412 crores.
….for 2016-17, we have asked for ` 1,800 crores. So, every year, we will have to
do it because of the production capacity of these companies. If we give them only for one
year , they will not be able to produce it.
3.15. The Committee appreciates the Commission’s initiative for phasing out old EVMs and
plan to procure new EVMs and VVPATs from BEL and ECIL for the upcoming General
Elections to the Lok Sabha in 2019. The Committee is of the view that with the every general
election more and more voters’ turn out is expected, as recently noticed in the assembly
elections in the States of Assam and West Bengal. Since periodic elections are the epitome
of democracy, the Committee feels that fund allocated may be revised for the procurement
of EVMs and VVPATs during the RE stage so that the work of Commission does not suffer.
BOGUS VOTERS AND D VOTER (DOUBTFUL VOTER)
3.16.  The National Electoral Roll Purification and Authentication Programme (NERPAP), popularly
known as ‘India Roll Call’ has been launched on 3
rd March, 2015 with the objectives (i) to link
and authenticate the EPIC data of electors with Aadhaar data (ii) voluntary disclosure of the
electors concerned of the multiple entries pertaining to them and disposal of such cases within 15
days by the Electoral Registration Officer (iii) correct the errors of any elector if it is there in the
entry of the EPIC and (iv) improvement of the image quality of the EPIC.
3.17.  The Election Commission of India in its written submission on the Demands for Grants
(2016-17) submitted that:
...The Commission before every Summary Revision undertakes pre-revision activities.
During these activities, EROs run de-duplication software in their ACs and after field
verification on the basis of the findings of software through BLOs, multiple entries are
removed. The electors having multiple entries in electoral roll have been given option to

16
disclose the information voluntarily. During NERP AP , an initiative was also undertaken to
integrate Aadhar no. of electors with electoral database but in light of the Interim Order
of Hon’ble Supreme court in WP (Civil) No. 494 of 2012, the Commission suspended “all
further activities relating to collection/feeding/seeding of Aadhar number under NERP AP
with immediate effect till further directions”.
3.18. The names of those persons whose Indian citizenship was in question were to be referred
to the concerned Tribunals, for final decision of the Tribunals set-up under the Foreigners
(Tribunals) order, 1964. Meanwhile, those names were to be provisionally included in the electoral
rolls but the word ‘doubtful’ was to be indicated against such names in the relevant portion of the
electoral roll under the footnote “D” meaning doubtful/disputed. After the receipt of the final
decision from the concerned Tribunal, the Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) shall either delete
or allow remaining such names in the electoral rolls in accordance with the above cited said Court
order. During the pendency of their cases, “D” voters were not allowed to vote. As per the latest
figure furnished by CEO Assam  there are 136448 number of persons in the  Electoral Roll which
are the marked as ‘D’  Doubtful voter.
3.19. The Committee appreciates the work of Election Commission of India in checking
bogus voting by electoral role purification by linking it with Aadhar card. The Committee
feels that a common electoral roll will reduce cost, time and check electoral malpractices
in the country. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a common electoral be
prepared in the country which can be used from panchayat level to Parliamentary elections
with the State Election Commissions  to weed out multiple electoral rolls to check corrupt
practices during elections. The Committee also recommends the ECI to ensure that no
persons voting rights are hampered by wrongfully categorizing them as Doubtful voters as
it will go against the very principle of electoral democracy.
3.20. The Committee recommends to the ECI to consolidate all the guidelines into a
simplified ‘code’ and publish the same for the knowledge of all the stakeholders. It has
been observed that ‘Citizens’ and their family members are often harassed by stooping their
vehicle and their privacy is also eroded in the name of implementation of the electoral code
of conduct despite there being no evidence of any illegal activity. This calls for abundant
precaution on the part of implementing agencies.
3.21. As regards the resolution of disputes during elections, the Committee suggests that
cases registered during the period should be handled by Special Prosecutors and
Magistrates on a time bound manner.

B. FAMILY COURTS
6.7 The Family Courts Act, 1984 provides for establishment of Family Courts by the State
Governments in consultation with the High Courts with a view to promote conciliation and secure
speedy settlement of disputes relating to marriage and family affairs and for matters connected
therewith. Under Section 3(1)(a) of the Family Courts Act, it is mandatory for the State
Governments to set up a Family Court for every area in the State comprising a city or a town
whose population exceeds one million. In other areas of the States, the Family Courts may be set
up if the State Governments deems it necessary. There are 438 functional family courts in the
country .
6.8 Central financial assistance started in the year 2002-03 with a non-recurring grant @ ` 10
lakh per court provided by the Department of Justice to the concerned States/UTs for setting up
of Family Courts and the concerned States to provide matching share. A further provision of ` 5 lakh
per court per annum for meeting running expenditure on Family Courts with matching share from
the concerned States was also put in place. In BE (2016-17) a provision of ` 0.01 crore has been
made for Family Courts/Special Courts. However, the Department of Justice in its written
submission to the Committee on the Demands for Grants (2016-17) submitted that Non-Plan grant
to Family Courts has been discontinued from 2016-17.
6.9 The Committee is unable to understand the reasons for discontinuation of Non-Plan
grants to the Family Courts when only 438 Family Courts have been established so far in

strengthened but separate complexes be set-up which should not be too far from the regular
courts.

6.25 One of the thrust areas of NALSA includes delivery of legal aid to the poor and

various stakeholders during its study-visit to Nagpur Jail, Maharashtra observed that there
are serious lacunae in the legal aid delivery by the NALSA and State Legal Services
Authority (SLSA). The under trials were not given proper legal aid and the Committee
takes very serious note of it. The Committee accordingly, recommends NALSA to monitor
the activities of SLSAs in various States in the area of legal aid as non-delivery of proper
legal aid to the marginalised sections is contrary to the very objective for which NALSA was
established.
6.26 One of the activities of NALSA is to undertake and promote research in the field of
legal education. The Committee accordingly, recommends NALSA to undertake research in
legal aid and education with national law schools in the country to identify bottlenecks in
its programmes/schemes and also to promote legal aid education.
6.27 The court fee paid to panel lawyers is very low and is difficult for NALSA to attract
competent lawyers. Since NALSA has already constituted a Committee on the issue, the
Committee, feels that the fee of panel lawyers and defence lawyers should be raised
reasonably and revise it periodically so that quality legal aid services can be provided to the
poor litigants.
6.28 The Committee feels that the Government should be in a position to appoint defense
lawyer at par with Prosecutor and Assistant Prosecutor (cadre appointee) to work under the

should be maintained to give instruction and participate in legal consultation on bail, trial
and appeal matters by the visit of the NALSA lawyers. There should be a separate room
constructed by NALSA in every Jail for such consultation and the defense lawyers appointed
should have proper consultation with the prisoners before appearing on their behalf in
courts, as the present system of arguing cases without the instruction of clients and in the
absence of clients is against human rights and fundamental rights guaranteed by the
Constitution of India. The Committee is also of the view that NALSA should provide TA &

COMPUTERISATION OF DISTRICT AND SUBORDINATE COURTS
(i) e-Courts Mission Mode Project Phase-I
6.40 The e-Courts Integrated Mission Mode Project approved in the year 2010 is one of the
National e-Governance projects (NeGP), being implemented for ICT enablement of district and
subordinate Courts of the country and envisages computerisation of 14,249 District and
Subordinate courts by 31
st March, 2015.
6.41 The objective of the e-Courts project is to provide designated services to litigants, lawyers
and the judiciary. The project facilitates automation of case management workflow through use of
application software for activities such as Case Filing, Scrutiny, Registration, Case Allocation, Court
Proceedings, Details entry of a Case, Case Disposal & restoration, Transfer of Case, Pendency data
/Institution Registers, Court Diaries, Calculation of court fees etc. The national e-Courts portal
(http://www.ecourts.gov.in)  provides online services to litigants such as details of case registration,
cause list, case status, daily orders, and final judgments. Currently, litigants can access case status
information in respect of over 6.04 crore pending and decided cases and more than 2.41crore
orders/judgements pertaining to district and subordinate Courts.
6.43. The Department in its written submission stated that sites for all 14,249 courts (100%) have
been made ready for computerisation, out of which LAN has been installed at 13,643 courts
(95.75%), hardware at 13,436 courts (94.3%) and software at 13,672 courts (96%). The

45
Department also submitted that change management exercise has been completed in all the High
Courts and more than 18000 judicial officers and staffs have been trained in UBUNTU-Linux and
Management Information System (MIS). Video Conferencing (VC) was piloted in five districts
under the supervision of e-Committee of Supreme Court. Based on the experience of pilots, it was
decided in consultation with the e-Committee of Supreme Court of India to provide VC facilities
for 488 Court complexes and 342 jails out of which equipment has been delivered at 667 locations.
Apart from VC facilities being provided under the e-Courts Project, some States have already
implemented VC in courts from their own resources.
(ii) e-Courts Mission Mode Project Phase-II
6.43 The Government approved Phase II of the eCourts MMP in its meeting held on 16 th July,

CHARTERED HIGH COURTS AND USE OF REGIONAL LANGUAGE AS THE LANGUAGE OF
THE HIGH COURT
6.59 Article 348 of the Constitution deals with the Language to be used in the Supreme Court
and in the High Courts and for Acts, Bills, etc. Clause (1) (a) of the Article says that,
notwithstanding anything in the foregoing provisions of this Part, until Parliament by law otherwise
provides, all proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court should be in English.
However, it further says that, Notwithstanding anything in sub clause (a) of clause (1), the
Governor of a State may, with the previous consent of the President, authorise the use of the Hindi
language, or any other language used for any official purposes of the State, in proceedings in the
High Court having its principal seat in that State: Provided that nothing in this clause shall apply
to any judgment, decree or order passed or made by such High Court.
6.60 The Committee is given to understand that demands from the State of Rajasthan, Tamil
Nadu and Gujarat for use of regional languages as the language of High Court is pending with
Union Government and Supreme Court of India. Regional languages are in use for quite a long time
now in the Subordinate Courts of those states. A Committee under the then Chief Justice of High
Court of Madras, Justice Sathasivam has recommended for use of Tamil language in the High Court
of Madras provided that simultaneous interpretation of Tamil language into English for non-Tamil
speaking judges is made available in that court.

51
6.61 The Committee reiterates its recommendations contained in 75 th report on the
Demands for Grants (2015-16) wherein it observed that Article 348 provides for the use of
scheduled languages, other than English, with the consent of the Governor of the State. The
diversity of languages spoken and enumerated in the Constitution of India clearly brings
out the importance of different languages of the country. The Committee, accordingly, feels
that, scheduled languages other than English may be permitted to be used in the High
Courts, provided it is demanded by the concerned State Government.  The Committee is
further of the view that the consultation process with judiciary is not required as the
Constitutional provisions are amply clear on the use of Scheduled Languages in the High
Courts and accordingly, the use of Scheduled Languages should be decided as per mandate
of Article 348.
6.62 As regards the Bombay, Madras and Calcutta High Courts, the Committee is of the
view that the names of these High Courts may be respectively changed to the new names,
viz. ‘High Court of Maharashtra, Mumbai and Benches at Nagpur and Aurangabad; Tamil
Nadu High Court at Chennai and Bench at Madurai; and High Court of Kolkata, Bench at
Andaman, Port Blair’.  This will require a Constitutional Amendment. The Committee
recommends the Department to move a Bill in this regard so that names of these High
Courts are accordingly changed.
6.63 The Committee feels that the Government should find avenues to generate revenue
to meet expenditure required for infrastructure requirements, supporting staff, etc. in the
courts so as to make them self–sustainable. The Committee accordingly, reiterates its
recommendations contained in Seventy-fifth Report on Demands for Grants (2015-16) that
revenue should be raised from parties which can afford to pay higher court fee, especially
corporate houses for improving the basic amenities for Judges and infrastructure. The
surplus funds, if any, can also be utilised for improving the facilities of the subordinate
judiciary keeping in view that it is the sovereign duty of the Government to provide free
criminal justice.
6.64 The Committee feels that Government should make some efforts for raising the
percentage of women judges in the High Courts and the Supreme Court. The Committee
insists that ideally the strength of women judges should be around 50 per cent of the total
strength of the judges.

absence of clients is against human rights and fundamental rights guaranteed by the
Constitution of India. The Committee is also of the view that NALSA should provide TA and
DA to clients/advocates to discuss relevant issues on their pending cases in District/Sessions
Courts, High Courts and the Supreme Court. (Para 6.29)
The Committee is happy to notes that as against allocation of for ````` 562.99 crore in
BE (2015-16) the same has been released to various States by the Department. The
Committee also take note the justifications for lower allocation of ````` 600 crore BE (2016-
17) as against projections of ````` 1500 crore that due to enhanced devolutions of funds to the
States under the Fourteenth Finance Commission, the States are expected to enhance their
investment in the justice delivery. The Committee expects that States will contribute more
for justice delivery system. The Committee now hopes that States would now be in position
to allocate more resources on justice delivery system. (Para 6.36)

58
The Committee appreciates the activities undertaken under A2J Project and feels
that it will go a long way in achieving the objective of delivering justice to under-
represented communities in the country.  Since the project is only for a five year period
(2012-17), the Committee feels that still a lot has to be done in the country in the area
of justice delivery, especially for the marginalised and poor sections of the society. The
Committee also feels that the project may be linked with customary law and practices to
provide justice to tribal people in North-East. Therefore, the Committee recommends the
Department to continue and extend the project so that the project can be used as a platform
to bring about a synergy between regular justice system and customary law and practices
in the North-East India. (Para 6.40)
The Committee hopes that new Phase-II of the e-Court Mission Mode Project will
utilize its learning experiences from Phase–I of the project to overcome the lacunae. The
Committee hopes that the e-Court Mission Mode-II’s objective of enhanced ICT enablement
of courts through universal computerisation, use of cloud computing, digitization of case
records and enhanced availability of e-services through e-filing, etc. will make the Digital
India Programme of the Government a success as it emphasises on Citizen centric services
with a focus on Digital Infrastructure as a core utility to every citizen. (Para 6.45)
The Committee expresses its concern at the slow pace of establishment of Gram
Nyalayas  even after 7 years after the enactment of the Act. Till date only 10 States have
notified Gram Nayalayas, where highly populated States Like Uttar Pradesh has only
established 12 Gram Nayalayas till date. The Committee also feels that non-applicability on
Gram Nyalayas Act in Tribal Areas of certain States is one of the reasons for its non-
popularity. The Committee accordingly feels that Gram Nyalayas be also extended to Tribal
Areas so that these Gram Nyalayas become a link between the regular justice system and
Tribal justice system. (Para 6.50)
The Committee takes note that the Fourteenth Finance Commission has
recommended allocation as projected by the Department. The Committee hopes that the
Department will optimally utilize the funds earmarked under various heads and also
monitor the physical targets set up so as to reduce pendency and augment physical and
human resources of the judiciary. (Para 6.53)
The Committee is concerned with the large pendency of cases in Supreme Court and
High Courts. Approximately 45 per cent posts are vacant in High Courts as the Collegium
system have failed to fill-up vacancies in time. The Committee feels that without filling-up
these vacancies, it will not be possible for the High Courts to reduce its pendency as both
are closely related. (Para 6.59)
     The Committee also reiterates its recommendations contained in its Thirty-ninth
Report on Demands for Grants (2010-11) and Eighty-Second Report on Action Taken Report
on the on the recommendations/ observations contained in the 75
th report on Demands for
Grants (2015-16), that the retirement age of judges of High Courts be increased to 65 years
to bring it at par with the retirement age of judges of Supreme Court of India by effecting
amendment to the Constitution and related legislation(s) so as to help in easing the
pressure of mounting vacancies in High Courts by passing the Bill. (Para 6.60)

59
The Committee reiterates its recommendations contained in 75 th Report on the
Demands for Grants (2015-16) wherein it observed that Article 348 provides for the use of
Scheduled languages, other than English, with the consent of the Governor of the State. The
diversity of languages spoken and enumerated in the Constitution of India clearly brings
out the importance of different languages of the country. The Committee, accordingly, feels
that, scheduled languages other than English may be permitted to be used in the High
Courts, provided it is demanded by the concerned State Government.  The Committee is
further of the view that the consultation process with judiciary is not required as the
Constitutional provisions are amply clear on the use of Scheduled Languages in the High
Courts and accordingly, the use of Scheduled Languages should be decided as per mandate
of Article 348. (Para 6.63)
As regards the Bombay, Madras and Calcutta High Courts, the Committee is of the
view that the names of these High Courts may be respectively changed to the new names,
viz. ‘High Court of Maharashtra, Mumbai and Benches at Nagpur and Aurangabad; Tamil
Nadu High Court at Chennai and Bench at Madurai; and High Court of Kolkata, Bench at
Andaman, Port Blair’. This will require a Constitutional Amendment. The Committee
recommends the Department to move a Bill in this regard so that names of these High
Courts are accordingly changed. (Para 6.64)
The Committee feels that the Government should find avenues to generate revenue
to meet expenditure required for infrastructure requirements, supporting staff, etc. in the
courts so as to make them self–sustainable. The Committee accordingly, reiterates its
recommendations contained in Seventy-fifth Report on Demands for Grants (2015-16) that
revenue should be raised from parties which can afford to pay higher court fee, especially
corporate houses for improving the basic amenities for Judges and infrastructure. The
surplus funds, if any, can also be utilised for improving the facilities of the subordinate
judiciary keeping in view that it is the sovereign duty of the Government to provide free
criminal justice. (Para 6.65)
The Committee feels that Government should make some efforts for raising the
percentage of women judges in the High Courts and the Supreme Court. The Committee
insists that ideally the strength of women judges should be around 50 per cent of the total
strength of the judges. (Para 6.66)
The Committee takes note of the justification furnished by the Supreme Court for
their projected demands of ````` 200 crore, including payments related to security issues and
recommends that budgetary allocations of the Supreme Court of India may be enhanced in
RE (2016-17) so as to meet its requirements of funds. (Para 7.3)

REPORT
CHAPTER–I
OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
The management of personnel policies in the Government of India, to begin with, was the
joint responsibility of the Ministry of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and Ministry
of Finance (Establishment Division), with Union Public Service Commission playing an important
advisory role. The Establishment Officer to the Government of India, functioning under the Cabinet
Secretary, had an important role to play in the senior level appointments under the Government of
India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified central direction.
1.1 To plug this organisational loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha, in
its 93
rd Report (April 1966) had observed that “the ever expanding role of the Government in a
welfare State with its natural concomitant of a large civil service calls for effective personnel
control through a single agency”. The Administrative Reforms Commission (ARC) too urged upon
the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel with a full fledged Secretary-in-
charge, to be placed directly under the Prime Minister to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel
functions of the Government.
1.2 The Union Government accepted this recommendation, and as a consequence, led to the
reorganization of the Ministry of Home Affairs as it then stood, resulting eventually in the formation
of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, as it stands today.  This process was
initiated on June 26, 1970 when the Department of Personnel was notified as a department in the
Cabinet Secretariat.  The process was taken further on August 1, 1970 with the notification of the
items of work to be dealt with by the Department.  Eventually, on March 15, 1985, a full fledged
‘Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions’ was notified.
1.3 The Ministry is the coordinating agency of the Central Government in personnel matters,
especially the issues concerning recruitment, promotion and morale of services, training, vigilance
and discipline, career development and service conditions of the middle and senior level
management, grievances and staff welfare, as well as the process of responsive people–oriented
modern administration.  The Ministry comprises three Departments, namely: -
(i) Department of Personnel and Training;
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances; and
(iii) Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare.
1.4 The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister, assisted by a Minister of
State. The Department of Personnel and Training is functioning under the charge of an independent
Secretary while the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances and Department
of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare functions under the charge of a Secretary.

2
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING
2. The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided into two
parts.  In its larger nodal role, it acts as the formulator of policy and the watchdog of Government,
ensuring that certain accepted standards and norms as laid down by it, are followed by all
Ministries/Departments in the recruitment, regulation of service conditions and deputation of
personnel, as well as other related issues. Towards this end, guidelines are issued by it for the
benefit of all the Ministries/Departments and it monitors implementation of these guidelines.  It also
advises all organisations of the Central Government on issues of personnel management.  At a more
immediate level, the Department has the direct responsibility of being the cadre controlling authority
for the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS). The
Department also operates the Central Staffing Scheme under which suitable officers from All India
Services and Group ‘A’ Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at the level of
Deputy Secretary, Director and Joint Secretary, on the basis of tenure deputation. The Department
also deals with cases of appointment to posts of Chairmen, Managing Directors, full-time functional
Directors/Members of the Board of Management of various public sector undertakings/enterprises,
corporations, banks and financial institutions.  It also deals with the assignment of Indian experts
to various developing countries.
Recruitment Agencies
3. The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of personnel for
Government are the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and the Staff Selection Commission
(SSC). The former is constituted under a provision of the Constitution and is responsible for
conducting examinations for appointment to the higher civil services and civil posts under the Union
Government, including recruitment to the All India Services. There is a mandatory provision for
consulting the Commission on all matters relating to methods of  recruitment, principles to be
followed in making promotions and transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary
matters. The SSC is responsible for making recruitment for Group ‘B’ non-gazetted posts of
Assistants, Stenographers, etc.
Training Institutions
4. Two major training institutions, directly under the administrative control of the Department,
are the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie and the
Institute of Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. The former is mainly
responsible for providing induction training to recruits to the Indian Administrative Service and
other All India Services and Central Services. The Institute of Secretariat Training and Management
provides induction as well as in-service training to members of the Central Secretariat Service.
Senior Appointments under the Government of India
5. All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the
approval of Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) under the Government of India
(Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961 are processed through the Establishment Officer as
Secretary to the ACC.  These include board level appointments to Central Public Sector
Undertakings and appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the

3
Ministries/Departments. In addition, all appointments by promotion, which require approval of the
ACC, are also processed through the Establishment Officer.
Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB)
6. The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making
recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executive and
functional Director and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Undertakings.
Administrative Vigilance
7. The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for maintenance
of integrity of the public services and eradication of corruption, and coordinates the activities of
various Ministries/Departments in that area.
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC): Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central
Vigilance Commission. It has jurisdiction and powers in respect of all matters to which the
executive power of the Union Government extends. The Commission is also entrusted with the
supervision of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).
The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: The Act has been brought into force with effect from
16th January, 2014. The Department is entrusted with the administration of the Act.
Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
8. The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is the premier investigating police agency in the
country, created through a resolution of Ministry of Home Affairs dated April 1, 1963 administering
Delhi Special Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, its jurisdiction covering all the Departments
of the Government of India, Union Territories, which could be extended to the States also with
the consent of the State Governments concerned. In due course, with the setting up of a large
number of Public Sector Undertakings, the employees of those undertakings were also brought
under the purview of CBI. Similarly, with the nationalization of the Banks in 1969, the Public
Sector Banks and their employees also came within the ambit of the CBI.  By now, the CBI has
become multi-disciplinary investigative agency, with its role expanding from corruption cases to
other cases viz- cyber crimes, terrorist crimes, wildlife crimes, narcotics, arms trafficking, arts and
antiquities cases, counterfeiting of currencies etc.
Joint Consultative Machinery
9. A well structured three-tier machinery is in place for joint consultation between the Central
Government and its employees for promoting harmonious relations and securing the greatest
measure of cooperation between the Central Government and the general body of employees in
matters of common concern. The objective is to increase the efficiency of public services along
with the well-being of the employees. The three tiers of JCM are:
(i) National Council- at the apex level, functioning under the Department of Personnel
and Training;
(ii) Department Councils- functioning at Ministries’/Departments’ level; and
(iii) Office Councils- functioning at offices/ organisations under various Ministries/
Departments.

4
Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
10. In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by the
Government decisions, Government had set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CA T) in 1985,
which deals with all the cases relating to service matters of Central Government employees.
Right to Information
11. The Department is entrusted with the administration of the Right to Information Act, 2005
and Rules including amendment thereof. The Department also overlooks the administration of the
Central Information Commission including selection of Chief Information Commissioner and
Information Commissioners.
Staff Welfare
12. The Department of Personnel and Training is intimately involved in various staff welfare and
other role led activities.  Mention in this connection can be made of the institution of Grih Kalyan
Kendra (a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860), the Kendriya Bhandar (a
registered cooperative society set up in 1963) and the Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports
Board (a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860).
12.1. The Department also supports various programmes, which are provided in various
Ministries/Departments, Central Government Employees Welfare Coordination Committee in Central
Government offices located outside Delhi, Residents’ Welfare Associations/Area Welfare Officers,
Benevolent Fund and Departmental Canteens.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEV ANCES
13. The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of
the Government of India for administrative reforms, as well as for redressal of public grievances
relating to the State in general and grievances pertaining to Central Government agencies in
particular. The Department disseminates information on important activities of Government relating
to administrative reforms and public grievances redressal through Management Publications and
Documentation. This Department also acts as the nodal agency in regard to Organisation and
Methods activities and offers advice to the Ministries/Departments. It also undertakes activities in
the field of international co-operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms.
13.1. This Department has, in the past few years, taken several initiatives with a view to bring
about improvement in the functioning and effectiveness of Government Departments, important
ones being the following:
(i) drawing up an agenda for reforms to be carried out in the Central Government as
well as in States; and
(ii) undertaking, through a Commission, a review of administrative laws which have
become obsolete and no longer need to be in the statute book.
13.2.  The Department also initiated an exercise on the part of Departments having public interface
to draw up their individual Citizen’s Charter to indicate the commitments of that organization for

5
quality and the time-frame in which services performed by that organization would be completed
for members of the public.
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
14. The Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare is the nodal agency of the
Government of India for formulation of general policy on pension and other retirement benefits, as
also for redressal of grievances relating to retirement benefits.  The Department was set up in 1985
as  part of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions and has been rendering service
for the benefit of pensioners since then.  The Department has taken a number of steps over the
years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater convenience and welfare of
the pensioners.
14.1 This Department, does not deal directly with pensioners but is the focal point for dealing
with issues concerning pensioners, and for issue of instructions and guidelines regarding matters
pertaining to pensioners.
14.2 The main responsibilities entrusted to this Department are:
(i) Formulation of policies and coordination of matters relating to retirement benefits of
Central Government employees, including Defence and Railways;
(ii) Administration of :
(a) Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972;
(b) Central Civil Services (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981;
(c) Central Civil Services (Extraordinary Pensions) Rules 1939;
(d) General Provident Fund (Civil Services) Rules, 1960; and
(e) Contributory Provident Fund (India) Rules, 1962;
(iii) Pension policy structure;
(iv) Examination and extending the scope of new facilities for fringe benefits to the
Central Government Pensioners;
(v) Matters relating to amendments to or relaxation of Pension Rules or any other rules
concerning retirement benefits; and
(vi) Policy and coordination relating to welfare of Central Government Pensioners/Family
Pensioners.

CHAPTER-III
POLICIES, PROGRAMMES  AND SCHEMES OF THE MINISTRY
30. The Committee, while examining the Demands for Grants (2016-17) of the Ministry also
made detailed study of the following recent policies, programmes and schemes undertaken by the
Departments under it.
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING
(i) Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI)
31. The foremost investigative police agency in the country and involved in major criminal
probes and is the interpolagency, the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has Plan schemes such
as ‘ Modernisation of Training Centre ’ of CBI intended for improvement of training facilities in CBI
Academy and its Regional Training Centres and modernization in Information Technology, strategic
options, re-engineering of process, up-gradation of training system, logistic and support facilities,
scientific and forensic support services and human resource management; ‘ e-governance ’ to equip
the field formations with modern equipments in order to fasten the enquiries; construction of a
state-of-the-art building is on at CGO complex, New Delhi to house the CBI Head Quarters; and
purchase of land from the MMRDA, Mumbai for accommodating the CBI Mumbai branch.
30.1 The Plan Outlay for the CBI in BE(2016-17) has been ` 75.00 crore as against ` 85.07
crore in BE (2015-16) which was reduced to ` 75.25 crore at the RE stage.
30.2 During the examination of the Demands for Grants (2016-17), the Director of CBI had
informed the Committee that during the last one year, the CBI has been taking steps to improve
its impact in the fight against corruption and investigation of crimes. The focus in the recent past
has been on modernizing and re-shaping its organization, capacity enhancement and upgradation of
skills of its manpower to meet the challenges of the 21 st century. With the recommendation of this
Committee in it’s 76 th Report to not compromise on funds projected for the plan scheme for
modernization of the CBI, the allocation for the Plan schemes of the CBI has remained the same.
However, the funds earmarked are inadequate and therefore, requested for additional funds.
30.3 The Committee strongly recommends for making adequate funds available to the
CBI to enable it to implement its Plan schemes to the ideal stipulation. The Committee is
however unable to understand why the allocation  of ````` 85.07 BE (2015-16) was reduced   to
````` 75.25 crore at the RE stage and then to ````` 75.00 crore as BE this year. The Committee
however surmises that fund reductions could be for the reason that the spending units, CBI
in this case, were unable to utilise 50% of the funds within the first six months of the
financial year, hence funds got reduced at next year’s BE. The Committee apprehends that
such a reduction may affect the pace of implementation of schemes. The Ministry in their
action taken replies should clarify the same, explain the reasons for such reductions and
17

18
also suggest how it can be avoided. Meanwhile, the Committee recommends to the CBI to
beef up the pace of the implementation of its proposed schemes.
30.4 The Committee noted from the  written replies to the questionnaire on Demands for Grants
(2016-17) submitted to the Committee the alarming number of vacancies across the various areas
of posts in the CBI, viz., 21% Executive Officers, 28% Legal Officers, 58% Technical Officers,
17% Ministerial Staff and 37 Canteen Staffs which are after the personnel engaged on contract
basis included in the Actual Strength in position. In response to the query on the pendency of
cases, the Committee was informed that as on 29.02.2016, CBI has a total number of 1200 cases
pending under investigation. Out of these, 31 cases are pending for more than three years. During
the interaction of the Committee with the Director, CBI, a Member also pointed out the 62 Foreign
Investigations pending with the CBI.
30.5 While deposing before the Committee, the Director, CBI proposed to provide longer tenure
to the officers on deputation in the CBI from the State and other Central forces in addition to the
other steps taken to manage the vacancy position. He further apprised the Committee that the
capacity of the CBI for investigation was around 700 cases a year which has now almost doubled
and as such more officers to supervise the investigation is needed. He also assigned the influx of
numerous cases to CBI partially due to the many cases referred by the States as they are over-
burdened with large number of cases instituted with them and also by orders of the Supreme Court
and High Courts. He therefore, expressed that unless the State Governments provide the manpower
by way of sending more of their personnel on deputation to the CBI, a time could come that the
CBI would collapse and fail. He further stressed the need for capacity building of their counterpart
State Police forces which he felt would go a long way in checkingthe inflow of cases to CBI.
30.6 On the query relating to officers of gazetted rank of the Government of India and public
sector undertakings suspected to be indulging in corruption vis-a-vis the time taken to complete
investigation, the Director informed that 2411 such officers have been identified which is an
increase of 87% over the last year. As regards the time taken for investigations, the duration range
from six months in small cases which can go upto one year in bigger cases. There are also some
very complex cases which may necessitate the investigation to go beyond a year. Since the
prosecution in the Courts depends on the evidence presented, there is no scope to either delete a
process to unduly hasten the process which could adversely effect the investigation.
30.7 The Committee expresses deep concern on the state of affairs relating to the vacancy
position in the CBI. It therefore impresses upon the DoPT to complete the exercise of cadre
review by June, 30, 2016 as per the direction of the Supreme Court to deal with the vacancy
position of the establishment. The Committee is apprehensive that unless the present
malady of massive vacancy is not corrected immediately, the very purpose of establishment
of the CBI would be eroded and its credibilitytarnished.  At this juncture when the nation
envisage the premier investigating agency of the country to be at par with their
international counterparts,  performance and result oriented and equipped to combat the
challenges of international pressures of transnational terrorism, cyber-crimes and
corruption, the Committee is disheartened that the CBI is crippled with a very basic
requirement, shortage of manpower.

19
30.7.1 With cases being referred by States and Courts to the CBI for investigation, the
Committee acknowledges the burden of load bestowed upon it. However, it is of the
concerted views that, the CBI turn to the State or other Central Forces to plug the vacancy
in the establishment. It therefore, desires that the CBI manage its cadre more efficiently
and the DoPT should take holistic steps to hasten the part of recruitment in consultation
with the UPSC. For that matter, the Committee strongly recommends the DoPT to revisit
the 24
th Report of the Committee on ‘The Working of the Central Bureau of Investigation
(CBI)’ wherein, after an exhaustive examination and intensive study of the issues, had
recommended workable ways to strengthen the CBI which included an enactment for the
CBI.
30.7.2 The Committee endorses the need for capacity enhancement and skill development
of the CBI as well as its counterpart State Police Forces. It is of the firm belief that,
augmenting the prowess and competence of the State Police Forces parallel to the CBI will
go a long way in abating cases referred to it by the States and thereby relieving the work-
load of the agency. The Committee commends the role played by the International Centre
for Excellence and Investigation, Ghaziabad in the field of capacity building and encourages
more exposure in the international arena by way of holding more interactions with their
international counterparts through the Centre.
30.7.3 Keeping in view the high pendency of cases with the CBI and especially those of
Foreign Investigations which have a direct bearing on the country’s credibility, the
Committee recommends that the activities of the Centre should be expanded to provide a
continuous in-service training to the CBI personnel in order to hone the skill and expertise
of those engaged in the field of crime investigation. The Committee further recommends
that, if need be, more funds for the purpose may be made available to the CBI.

be adequately equipped not only in physical terms but also in terms of its manpower.  Due
to the fact that the whole system of governance is now changing and the international
pressure and expectations are now high, flexibility has to be brought into the system. In
that context, all training programmes confined to one location may not be the single answer

20
to the existing problem of shortage of manpower. Accordingly, other feasible options of
handling the situation may be explored. At the same time, the DoPT should evolve a policy
which can address this constraint of the LBSNAA.
31.3 As regards the reduction of funds of the LBSNAA, while acknowledging the
justification of the Ministry, the Committee is of the view that every spending unit should
make a prudent exercise of the avenues of actually carrying out plan schemes it proposes
to undertake before budgetary allocations are sought. Furthermore, strategies should be
drawn for the utilization of funds made available to spending units and should be closely
monitored.

(iv) Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT)
33. Pursuant to the provision of Article 323A of the Constitution of India, the Administrative
Tribunal Act, 1985 was enacted by Parliament, to set up Administrative Tribunals for adjudication
of disputes and complaints with regard to recruitment and conditions of service of persons

21
appointed to public services and posts, in connection with the affairs of the Union and the
States.
33.1. The non-Plan Budgetary allocation of ` 133.67 crore has been made at BE 2016-17 for CA T
while BE 2015-16 was ` 95.15 crore, RE 2015-16 was `95.73 and Actuals for 2015-16 was
` 91.16 crore. However, CAT has  no Plan component.
33.2. The Principal Registrar, CAT deposed before the Committee on Demands for Grants (2016-17)
during which she conveyed gratitude for the great concern and recommendation of the Committee
regarding Central Administrative Tribunal due to which allocation of ` 30 crores was made for
purchase of land and buildings. Sufficient funds for technology upgradation was also allotted in the
last two years and some major initiatives have been undertaken, viz., Case Information System and
Digitization. She went on to inform that the current requirement is additional space for Central
Administrative Tribunal Principal Bench which has been arranged in rented accommodation for the
Finance Wing to keep the records. Its location being at quite a distance causes  great constraint
on its functioning.  She also submitted that at present, CAT has no earmarked accommodation for
the hon. Chairman and hon. Members and there is shortage of Stenographic assistance . She further
submitted that for the smooth functioning of the Tribunal, additional benches need to be sanctioned
because there is a single bench in several places.
33.3. The Committee feels that CAT needs to be strengthened in terms of infrastructure
and also the human resource. Therefore, the Committee suggests the Ministry to resolve
the issues related therewith. The Committee also feels that the CAT should function as
mediator rather than a court or an appellate authority. Effort should be to avoid further
appeal against CAT decision   to the High Court or the Supreme Court.  The Committee,
however, suggests that even where it is felt that the law has not been properly applied,
review petition should be encouraged and the CAT should mediate till the case is settled.
33.4. The Committee is of the concerted opinion that employees frustrated with the service
condition approach Courts, including CAT where they end up waiting for years for the
judgement and thereby the entire system is adversely affected. The Committee feels that
many of the cases in service matters can be settled by mediation within the system itself.
The Committee is of the opinion that in the administration, the senior officer be made
duty-bound to resolve the grievances of the subordinate officers. He is expected to sit along
with the aggrieved and decide the matter, get the concurrence of the supreme authority and
complete the  entire  process.  The tribunals/ Courts are need to be resorted to  only in
the rarest matters. Thus, the Committee calls for a drastic change in the attitude of the
administration.

(viii) Fixed Tenure of IAS, IPS and IFS
37. In WP (C) No.82/2011 filed by Shri T.S.R. Subramanian & Ors. Vs UoI & Ors, the
Supreme Court in Judgment dated 31.10.2013 directed the Centre, State Governments and the

25
Union Territories to constitute Civil Services Boards (CSB) with high ranking serving officers, who
are specialists in their respective fields, within a period of three months, if not already constituted,
till the Parliament brings in a proper legislation in setting up CSB. In compliance of the Apex
Court’s directions, amendments in rule 7 of the IAS, IPS and IFS (Cadre) Rules have been carried
out vide notification dated 28.01.2014. Accordingly, the amended Rule 7 (3) of the Indian
Administrative Service (Cadre) Rules, 1954 states “ A cadre officer, appointed to any cadre post
shall hold the office for at least two years unless in the meantime he or she has been promoted,
retired or sent on deputation outside the State or training exceeding two months. ”
37.1. During the meeting of the Committee on Demands for Grants (2016-17), a Member
expressed his concern over the non compliance of certain States of Rule 7 (3) of the Indian
Administrative Service (Cadre) Rules, 1954. He stated that these States took the liberty of
transferring officers on their whims and pleasures overnight, in one month, two months and so
on and several times without even giving them prior notice. The Secretary, DoPT informed that
cases have been filed in Courts by the Officers and contempt petitions from Courts have also come
against certain States in this regard.
37.2. The Secretary further informed that the Department conducts a cadre review  every five
years during which cadre strength and other related issues are considered. States have also been
requested to inform the average tenure of high ranking Officers in service.
37.3. In this context the Committee views that the DoPT should impress upon the State
Governments to strictly comply with the service rules relating to tenure of the high ranking
Officers in service so that the Officers are able to discharge their duty without fear.
(ix) Recruitment Drive for Persons with Disabilities (PwD)
38. Reservation to Persons with Disabilities is provided in line with the provisions of the
Persons with Disabilities (Equal Opportunities, Protection of Rights and Full Participation) Act,
1995, in posts and services under the Government of India.
38.1. Three per cent of the vacancies in case of direct recruitment to Group A, B, C and D posts
shall be reserved for persons with disabilities of which one per cent each shall be reserved for
persons suffering from (i) blindness or low vision, (ii) hearing impairment and (iii) locomotor
disability or cerebral palsy in the posts identifies for each disability;
38.2. Three per cent of the vacancies in case of promotion to Group D and Group C posts in
which the element of direct recruitment, if any, does not exceed 75%, shall be reserved for persons
which disabilities of which one per cent each shall be reserved for persons suffereing from (i)
blindness or law vision, (ii) hearing impairment and (iii) locomotor disability or cerebral palsy in
the posts identified for each disability.
38.3. In it’s deposition on Demands for Grants (2016-17) before the Committee, the
representative of the DoPT highlighted the initiatives of the Department which include   thrust on
filling 15,831 vacancies in Central Government for ‘Divyaangs’ or physically challenged. She went
on to state that 10,903 vacancies have been filled up by a conducting a special recruitment drive
for Persons with Disabilities (PwD). 4,290 more vacancies are yet to be filled.

levels of excellence in administration in the present era of globalization within a set time-
frame. In this regard, the Committee recommends that, if the need be, higher budgetary
projections may be made at the RE stage under this component so that the completion of

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee appreciates the innovative move of  projecting all Plan Outlays of the
three Departments of the Ministry under a single Major Head, i.e. ‘2070’.  The move has
erased the chances of overlapping projections in the Minor Heads and Object Heads of the
projections. (Para 27)
The AS and FA of the Ministry had given justifications for the reduction of the funds
allocated for LBSNAA that the Academy did not make a fifty per cent utilization by
september of the financial year 2015-16 which led to the reduction of funds at the RE stage.
Further by the end of that financial year, the utilization was 85% of the total allocation and
therefore the budgetary allocation for 2016-17 has been reduced. However, the Committee
is the view that reduction of budgetary allocation reflects that the spending unit has not
assessed its targets thoroughly before making the projections. It, therefore, desires that
such instances of lapse should be avoided at all cost. The Committee, accordingly, desires
that all spending units of the Ministry may be required to furnish their respective
percentage of expenditure as on that date when furnishing the Action Taken Replies of this
Report. (Para 28)
The Committee is on the whole, in respect of fund management of the Ministry, is
happy with the performance of the Ministry. It however, wishes to recommend that every
Department should ensure that early commencement of its schemes/projects to ensure the
50% utilization of the funds before september of each year so as to avoid fund reduction
by the Ministry of Finance. (Para 29)
The Committee strongly recommends for making adequate funds available to the
CBI to enable it to implement its Plan schemes to the ideal stipulation. The Committee is
however unable to understand why the allocation  of ````` 85.07 BE (2015-16) was reduced   to
````` 75.25 crore at the RE stage and then to ````` 75.00 crore as BE this year. The Committee
however surmises that fund reductions could be for the reason that the spending units, CBI
in this case, were unable to utilise 50% of the funds within the first six months of the
financial year, hence funds got reduced at next year’s BE. The Committee apprehends that
such a reduction may affect the pace of implementation of schemes. The Ministry in their
action taken replies should clarify the same, explain the reasons for such reductions and
also suggest how it can be avoided. Meanwhile, the Committee recommends to the CBI to
beef up the pace of the implementation of its proposed schemes. (Para 30.3)
The Committee expresses deep concern on the state of affairs relating to the vacancy
position in the CBI. It therefore impresses upon the DoPT to complete the exercise of cadre
review by June, 30, 2016 as per the direction of the Supreme Court to deal with the vacancy
position of the establishment. The Committee is apprehensive that unless the present
malady of massive vacancy is not corrected immediately, the very purpose of establishment
32

33
of the CBI would be eroded and its credibility tarnished.  At this juncture when the nation
envisage the premier investigating agency of the country to be at par with their
international counterparts,  performance and result oriented and equipped to combat the
challenges of international pressures of transnational terrorism, cyber-crimes and
corruption, the Committee is disheartened that the CBI is crippled with a very basic
requirement, shortage of manpower. (Para 30.7)
With cases being referred by States and Courts to the CBI for investigation, the
Committee acknowledges the burden of load bestowed upon it. However, it is of the
concerted views that, the CBI turn to the State or other Central Forces to plug the vacancy
in the establishment. It therefore, desires that the CBI manage its cadre more efficiently
and the DoPT should take holistic steps to hasten the part of recruitment in consultation
with the UPSC. For that matter, the Committee strongly recommends the DoPT to revisit
the 24 th Report of the Committee on ‘The Working of the Central Bureau of Investigation
(CBI)’ wherein, after an exhaustive examination and intensive study of the issues, had
recommended workable ways to strengthen the CBI which included an enactment for the
CBI. (Para 30.7.1)
The Committee endorses the need for capacity enhancement and skill development
of the CBI as well as its counterpart State Police Forces. It is of the firm belief that,
augmenting the prowess and competence of the State Police Forces parallel to the CBI will
go a long way in abating cases referred to it by the States and thereby relieving the work-
load of the agency. The Committee commends the role played by the International Centre
for Excellence and Investigation, Ghaziabad in the field of capacity building and encourages
more exposure in the international arena by way of holding more interactions with their
international counterparts through the Centre. (Para 30.7.2)
Keeping in view the high pendency of cases with the CBI and especially those of
Foreign Investigations which have a direct bearing on the country’s credibility, the
Committee recommends that the activities of the Centre should be expanded to provide a
continuous in-service training to the CBI personnel in order to hone the skill and expertise
of those engaged in the field of crime investigation. The Committee further recommends that,
if need be, more funds for the purpose may be made available to the CBI. (Para 30.7.3)
The Committee expects that the premier training institution of the country ought to
be adequately equipped not only in physical terms but also in terms of its manpower.  Due
to the fact that the whole system of governance is now changing and the international
pressure and expectations are now high, flexibility has to be brought into the system. In
that context, all training programmes confined to one location may not be the single answer
to the existing problem of shortage of manpower. Accordingly, other feasible options of
handling the situation may be explored. At the same time, the DoPT should evolve a policy
which can address this constraint of the LBSNAA. (Para 31.2)
