REPORT
CHAPTER-I
OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
INTRODUCTION
1.0 The Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is the nodal Ministry responsible for
personnel matters, especially in respect of issues concerning recruitment, training, career development,
staff welfare and the post retirement dispensation. The Ministry also works towards promotion of
responsive, people-oriented and modern administration.
1.1 The Ministry comprises three Departments:
(i) Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT)
(ii) Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG)
(iii) Department of Pensions and Pensioners' Welfare (DPPW)
1.2 The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister, assisted by a Minister of State.
The Department of Personnel and Training is functioning under the charge of an independent Secretary
while the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances and Department of Pensions and
Pensioners' Welfare function under the charge of a Secretary.
EVOLUTION OF THE MINISTRY
1.3 The management of personnel policies in the Government of India, to begin with, was the joint
responsibility of the Ministry of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and Ministry of Finance
(Establishment Division), with Union Public Service Commission playing an important advisory role. The
Establishment officer to the Government of India, functioning under the Cabinet Secretary, had an
important role to play in the senior level appointments under the Government of India. All this made for
improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified central direction. To plug this organizational
loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha, in its 93rd Report (April 1966) had observed
that "the ever expanding role of the Government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large
civil service calls for effective personnel control through a single agency". The Administrative Reforms
Commission (ARC) too urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel with
a full fledged secretary-in-charge, to be placed directly under the Prime Minister to serve as a nodal
agency for the personnel functions of the Government.
1.4 The Union Government accepted this recommendation, and as a consequence, led to the
reorganization of the Ministry of Home Affairs as it then stood, resulting eventually in the formation of
Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, as it stands today. This process was initiated on
June 26, 1970 when the Department of Personnel was notified as a department in the Cabinet Secretariat.
The process was taken further on August 1, 1970 with the notification of the items of work to be dealt

2
with by the Department. Eventually, on March 15, 1985, a full fledged 'Ministry of Personnel, Public
Grievances and Pensions' was notified.
DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING (DoPT)
1.5 Various wings of DoP&T are as under:
(i) Establishment Officer's (EO) Wing- the Establishment Officer's Wing deals with the matter
relating to senior appointments under the Government of India requiring approval of the
Appointment Committee of Cabinet (ACC).
(ii) Services and Vigilance (S&V) Wing - the Services and Vigilance Wing handles matters
relating to cadre management of All India Services and acts as the nodal agency in the arena
of vigilance and anti-corruption. This wing in addition to governing the implementation of
RTI Act, also handles the administrative matters relating to the Administrative Tribunals and
Central Information Commission. This wing also handles the work related to cadre
restructuring in respect of the other Central Services.
(iii) Establishment (Estt.) Wing - The Establishment Wing is responsible for framing and revising
rules and regulations regarding service conditions of the employees and personnel policies
of the Central Government employees other than All India Service Officers. This wing also
handles the work related to Civil Services Officers' Institute (CSOI).
(iv) T raining (Trg.) Wing - The Training Wing acts as the nodal agency for training of Government
functionaries and is primarily responsible for formulating policies with regard to training.
(v) Administration Wing - Administration Wing deals with the matters related to cadre management
of the Central Secretariat Service, Central Secretariat Stenographers Service and the Central
Secretariat Clerical Service. This wing, also handles the administrative matters relating to
the State Re-organization, Reservation Policy of the Government and Welfare Activities for
benefit of the employees of the Government except CSOI.
1.6 The Department of Personnel and Training also handles the administrative work relating to the
following Institutions:
(i) Union Public Service Commission
(ii) Central Vigilance Commission
(iii) Lokpal
(iv) Central Administrative Tribunals
(v) Central Information Commission
(vi) Central Bureau of Investigation
(vii) Staff Selection Commission
(viii) Public Enterprises Selection Board

3
(ix) Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration
(x) Institute of Secretariat Training and Management
RECRUITMENT AGENCIES
1.7 The two organizations through which the Department ensures recruitment of personnel for
Government are the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and the Staff Selection Commission
(SSC). The former is constituted under a provision of the Constitution and is responsible for conducting
examinations for appointment to the higher civil services and civil posts under the Union Government,
including recruitment to the All India Services. There is a mandatory provision for consulting the
Commission on all matters relating to methods of recruitment, principles to be followed in making
promotions and transfers from one service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The SSC is
responsible for making recruitment for Group 'B' non-gazetted posts of Assistants, Stenographers, etc.
TRAINING INSTITUTIONS
1.8 Two major training institutions, directly under the administrative control of the Department, are
the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie and the Institute of
Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. The former is mainly responsible for providing
induction training to recruits to the Indian Administrative Service and other All India Services and Central
Services. The Institute of Secretariat Training and Management provides induction as well as in-service
training to members of the Central Secretariat Service.
SENIOR APPOINTMENTS UNDER THE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
1.9 All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the approval
of Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) under the Government of India (Transaction of
Business) Rules, 1961 are processed through the Establishment Officer as Secretary to the ACC. These
include board level appointments to Central Public Sector Undertakings and appointments of Joint
Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries/Departments. In addition, all appointments
by promotion, which require approval of the ACC, are also processed through the Establishment Officer.
PUBLIC ENTERPRISES SELECTION BOARD (PESB)
1.10 The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making
recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executive and functional
Director and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Undertakings.
ADMINISTRATIVE VIGILANCE
1.11 The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for maintenance of
integrity of the public services and eradication of corruption, and coordinates the activities of various
Ministries/Departments in that area.
Central Vigilance Commission: Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central
Vigilance Commission (CVC). It has jurisdiction and powers in respect of all matters to which the

4
executive power of the Union Government extends. The Commission is also entrusted with the
supervision of the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) so far offences investigated under the
Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 is concerned.
The Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: The Act has been brought into force with effect from
16th January, 2014. The Department is entrusted with the administration of the Act.
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
1.12 The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) is the premier investigating police agency in the country,
created through a resolution of Ministry of Home Affairs dated April 1, 1963 administering Delhi Special
Police Establishment (DSPE) Act, 1946, its jurisdiction covering all the Departments of the Government
of India, Union Territories, which could be extended to the States also with the consent of the State
Governments concerned. In due course, with the setting up of a large number of Public Sector
Undertakings, the employees of those undertakings were also brought under the purview of CBI. Similarly,
with the nationalization of the Banks in 1969, the Public Sector Banks and their employees also came
within the ambit of the CBI. By now, the CBI has become multi-disciplinary investigative agency, with
its role expanding from corruption cases to other cases viz cyber crimes, terrorist crimes, wildlife
crimes, narcotics, arms trafficking, arts and antiquities cases, counterfeiting of currencies etc.
JOINT CONSULTATIVE MACHINERY
1.13 A well structured three-tier machinery is in place for joint consultation between the Central
Government and its employees for promoting harmonious relations and securing the greatest measure of
cooperation between the Central Government and the general body of employees in matters of common
concern. The objective is to increase the efficiency of public services along with the well-being of the
employees. The three tiers of Joint Consultative Machinery (JCM) are:
(i) National Council- at the apex level, functioning under the Department of Personnel and
Training;
(ii) Department Councils- functioning at Ministries'/ Departments' level; and
(iii) Office Councils- functioning at offices/ organisations under various Ministries/ Departments.
CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
1.14 In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by the Government
decisions, Government had set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in 1985, which deals with
all the cases relating to service matters of Central Government employees.
RIGHT TO INFORMATION
1.15 The Department is entrusted with the administration of the Right to Information Act, 2005 and
Rules thereunder. The Department also overlooks the administration of the Central Information Commission
including selection of Chief Information Commissioner and Information Commissioners.

5
STAFF WELFARE
1.16 The Department of Personnel and Training is intimately involved in various staff welfare and other
role led activities. Mention in this connection can be made of the institution of Grih Kalyan Kendra (a
society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860), the Kendriya Bhandar (a registered cooperative
society set up in 1963) and the Central Civil Services Cultural and Sports Board (a society registered
under the Societies Registration Act, 1860).
1.17 The Depart ment also supports various programmes, which are provided in various Ministries/
Departments, Central Government Employees Welfare Coordination Committee in Central Government
offices located outside Delhi, Residents' Welfare Associations/Area Welfare Officers, Benevolent Fund
and Departmental Canteens.
INDIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION
1.18 Department of Personnel and Training also provides grant-in-aid to Indian Institute of Public
Administration (IIPA), New Delhi which undertakes research studies on contemporary public issues and
provides training to officers of Government of India on public policy.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEV ANCES
1.19 The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG) is the nodal agency
of the Government of India for administrative reforms as well as redressal of public grievances relating
to the States in general and those pertaining to Central Government agencies in particular. The Department
endeavors to document and disseminate successful governance practices by way of audiovisual media
and publications. The Department also undertakes activities in the field of international exchange and
cooperation to promote public service reforms. The Department is headed by the Secretary, Department
of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances and Pensions and Pensioners' Welfare. Available staff
strength is one secretary, one Additional secretary, two Joint Secretaries, 6 Directors/Deputy Secretaries
and 16 Under Secretary level officers in the Department. There are 7 Divisions in the Department namely
Administrative Reforms, Organization and Methods, e-Governance, Documentation and Dissemination,
International Exchange and Cooperation, Administration and Coordination and Public Grievances.
1.20 As per the Government of India Allocation of Business Rules, 1961 the following subjects have
been allotted to the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances:
(i) Administrative Reforms, including e-governance and dissemination of best practices.
(ii) organization and Methods.
(iii) Policy, coordination and monitoring of issues relating to —
(a) Redress of public grievances in general; and
(b) Grievances pertaining to Central Government agencies.
(iv) Research in public management and Liaison with State Governments, professional institutions
etc. in public management matters.
(v) Administration of Central secretariat Manual of office Procedure.

6
1.21 Functions of the Department are given as under:
(i) Matters relating to administrative reforms.
(ii) Or ganization of Civil Services Day and Inter Services Workshops.
(iii) Capacity building, change management and Government Process Re-engineering to provide
reform through e-Governance.
(iv) E-office Mission Mode Project under NeGP.
(v) Organization of National Conference on e-Governance and National awards on e-Governance.
(vi) Management of Public Grievance Redressal Mechanism.
(vii) Documentation and dissemination of Good Governance Practices — innovations, adaptation
and replication.
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND PENSIONERS' WELFARE (DPPW)
1.22 The Department of Pension and Pensioners' Welfare was set up in 1985 as part of the Ministry
of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions to formulate policy and coordination of matters relating
to retirement benefits of Central Government employees (including Defence and Railway Pensioners).
1.23 The main functions of this Department are:
(i) Formulation of policies and coordination of matters relating to retirement benefits of Central
Government employees, including Defence and Railways;
(ii) Administration of:
(a) Central Civil Services (Pension) Rules, 1972;
(b) Central Civil Services (Commutation of Pension) Rules, 1981;
(c) Central Civil Services (Extraordinary Pensions) Rules 1939;
(d) General Provident Fund (Civil Services) Rules, 1960; and
(e) Contributory Provident Fund (India) Rules, 1962;
(iii) Pension policy structure;
(iv) Examination and extending the scope of new facilities for fringe benefits to the Central
Government Pensioners;
(v) Matters relating to amendments to or relaxation of Pension Rules or any other rules concerning
retirement benefits; and
(vi) Policy and coordination relating to welfare of Central Government Pensioners/Family
Pensioners.

Vacancies in the Indian Administrative Service (IAS)
3.1 Indian Administrative Service (IAS) is the premier service of Government of India. The IAS has
been a hallmark of governance in India and has been manning the key and strategic positions throughout
the Union of India. Sardar Vallabhai Patel, one of the eminent leaders of the freedom struggle referred
to them as the steel frame of the country. The cadre controlling authority of the IAS is DoPT.

Civil List as on 1.1.2016 for IAS and incumbency position is as under:

3.3 The Committee was informed that out of 1470 vacancies, about 900 vacancies are from the Direct
Recruitment quota and rest from States promotion quotas. The Secretary, DoPT, in his presentation
before the Committee also informed that 900 direct recruitment shortfall is primarily due to two reasons.
One reason is that the cadre review has been done very recently and the number of posts has gone up.
The second one is, for ten years in the past, the recruitment was abnormally low. These two factors
resulted in shortfall in the direct recruitment. He further stated that the direct recruitment cannot be
stepped up all of a sudden as the training capacity for IAS officers is only 180 per year. Moreover, if
large number of officers are inducted in one go, there would be problem of cadre management. The
DoPT had set up B.S. Baswan Committee and that Committee recommended that it would not be
appropriate to increase the annual intake of IAS beyond 180 as it would compromise quality, exceed
LBSNAA's capacity and lead to distortion in career pyramid of IAS officers. Every year, 120 directly
recruited officers retire and as a result of this, effectively only 60 officers are added every year to the
IAS.
3.4 On a perusal of Annual Report 2016-17 of the Ministry, the Committee observes that
shortage of IAS officers in this Country has been a perennial problem since 1951. But now the
vacancy position has increased to an alarming level. With the present rate of recruitment it will
require decades to fill the existing vacancies. The Committee notes that almost all the key and
22

strategic positions under the Union as well as the States are being manned by the IAS and
persistent shortage in the IAS officers ultimately affects governance in the country. The Committee
expresses its serious concern over persistent shortage of IAS officers and strongly recommends
that all efforts be made to fill these vacancies. The Committee further notes that the Director,
LBSNAA has informed it that Academy has the capacity to train more than 180 officers, it,
therefore, fails to understand as to why lack of training capacity has been cited as one of the
reasons for not filling the vacancies of IAS officers. The Committee feels lack of training
capacity should not become a reason for non-filling of vacancies of IAS officers and if we are
actually short of capacity in this regard, efforts should be made to enhance our capacity to train
more IAS officers and that should not be a difficult to achieve.

Public Grievance Redressal & Public Service Delivery
3.71 The Department is entrusted with the responsibility for policy, coordination and monitoring of
issues relating to (a) Redress of Public Grievances in general and (b) Grievances pertaining to Central
Government Agencies, in particular. The Public Grievance Division of the Department is responsible for
this activity since December 1987. From 1997, the Division has also been made responsible for several
citizen centric initiatives under the platform of 'Responsive Government'. These include Citizens' Charter,
Information Facilitation Counters (IFC), and Quality Management System (QMS) framework called
Sevottam, for bringing improvement in public service delivery on a continuous basis, which may result
in Certification under Indian Standard 15700:2005 by Bureau of Indian Standards.
3.72 The management of public grievances envisages reduction in grievances, by bringing continuous
improvement in Public Service Delivery through the extension of Quality Management System ‘Sevottam’
at the Centre as well as in the States. Statutory backing for improvements in service delivery was sought
to be given through the 'Right of Citizens For Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal
of Their Grievances Bill, 2011 ’ that had been introduced in the Lok Sabha on 20.12.2011. It lapsed with
the dissolution of 15th Lok Sabha. The Department informed the Committee that it is now proposed to
implement a Scheme for Delivery of Services and Redress of Public Grievances.

42
3.73 An online system for grievance redress, called the 'Centralized Public Grievance Redress and
Monitoring System' (CPGRAMS) has evolved since 2007. It was submitted to the Committee that at
present its upgraded version 5.0 is accessible at http://pgportal.gov.in and also through www.darpg.gov.in.
It interlinks 139 Ministries/Departments/States/UTs and other apex organizations in CPGRAMS. There
are 26400 sub-ordinate users listed on it which includes subordinate and field offices also. The Committee
was further informed that the number of subordinate users linked to CPGRAMS has increased from
about 1500 in 2010-11 to over 26000 in 2016-17. CPGRAMS is also available in Hindi.
3.74 The Department in their written submission to the Committee has informed that 10.23 Lakh
grievances were received during 2016, out of which 7.53 Lakh grievances were redressed during the
said period.
3.75 Out of total budget under Plan Scheme for Administrative Reforms of ` 29.53 crore, ` 1.80 crore
has been projected for Centralized Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS) during
2017-18. The Department has also proposed to utilize the allocation for the Project Management unit
(PMU) established for monitoring systemic reforms for reducing grievances and improving public service
delivery. A Project for complete revamp of CPGRAMS with many new features like lateral transfer of
grievances, downward transfer of grievances from Ministries to State Governments provision of local
language interface, Dashboards etc. is also under consideration of the Department.
3.76 Dealing with the grievances of citizen effectively is one of the core components of Good
Governance. CPGRAMS is a good initiative of the Government for redressal of citizen grievances.
However, public at large, particularly those who are living in rural and far-flung areas needs to
be made aware of existence of such grievance redressal system. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that this system of Public Grievance Redressal (CPGRAMS) should be publicized in
mass media in vernacular languages, so that common people become aware of availability of such
avenue for redressal of their grievances against the Government organisations.
3.77 The Committee feels that the spirit of Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism is primarily
to resolve the grievances in a professional and satisfactory manner. The relief and remedial
mechanism need to fix the accountability on the decision making authorities. As in the event of
unsatisfactory redressal of their grievances, the public usually approach courts for redressal of
their grievances which increases burden of courts, every endeavour should be made that grievances
are resolved in a professional and satisfactory manner.
3.78 In order to make grievance redressal system (CPGRAMS) more effective, it is recommended
that Government may also consider making a provision for appeal in the existing system.
3.79 The Committee also takes note of the fact that over the time there has been a substantial
increase in the number of public grievances received by the Department. The Committee desires
that all those areas where large number of grievances are received, are examined and in those
common areas of grievances, after analyzing the root cause, systemic changes should be brought
in to reduce the volume of grievances pertaining to them. Also, suo-motu information relating
to those areas should be largely publicized on the Department's website, news papers and other
such media.

43
3.80 Further, as of now, 21 States/UTs have enacted statute for time bound delivery of services.
The Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redress of their
Grievances Bill, 2011 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 20th December, 2011. However, it could
not be passed and lapsed with the dissolution of the 15th Lok Sabha. The Committee feels that
Delivery of Government Services and Grievance Redressal should have statutory backing. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should consider re-introduction of the
said Bill in the year 2017-18.

Committee hopes that maximum number of pensioners will be benefited by these services. The
Committee, at the same time would like the Department to make more efforts to reach out to
its primary stakeholders i.e.  pensioners and especially family pensioners about the latest
developments and changes brought about in entitlements including the additional facility of
submission of Aadhaar based Digital Life Certificate. As more funds have been allocated to the
Department for BE (2017-18) towards publicity and advertisement, the Committee hopes that
Department would ensure that its schemes reach to the target groups i.e. pensioners staying in
every nook and corner  of the country.
3.91 The Committee also notes that pensions are generally disbursed through Public Sector
Banks and many a time the banks do not disburse pension timely and correctly. Pensioners are
at times harassed by these banks and their grievances with them remain unresolved. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that Department should also take up the matter with these
banks, so that the pensioners' grievances pertaining to the disbursing banks, are also satisfactorily
resolved.
3.92 The Committee feels that filling of pension forms and pension procedures still remain
complicated, even though some welcome steps have been taken by the Department in this
regard. The Committee recommends that number of pension forms should be further rationalized/
reduced and simplified. For this, the Department may consider taking the services of National
Centre for Good Governance (NCGG). The Department may also provide option of filling online
application for pension and other pensionary benefits.

46
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee after analyzing the trend of expenditure in the 2016-17 in the Departments
of this Ministry and their organizations observes that as on 31st January, 2017 the Ministry has
been able to spend only about 70% of the funds under plan schemes. Thus, performance of the
Departments in terms of utilization of funds under plan schemes leaves much to be desired. The
reasons cited by the Ministry for under-utilization of funds are administrative and procedural
which could have been avoided. This also shows that a focused planning and close monitoring of
utilization of funds, is required on part of the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Ministry should identify the bottlenecks responsible for not being able to utilize optimally
the funds at its disposal and take remedial measures so as to improve its performance in
utilization of plan funds in the future. (Para 2.50)
The Department of Personnel and Training and bodies/organizations under its administrative
control play a very important role in the personnel management under Government of India and
in the governance of the country. The Ministry was allocated for FY 2016-17 under plan schemes
````` 250.00 crore at BE stage and ````` 258.00 crore at RE stage. Even for the BE (2017-18) only
````` 340.00 crore has been allocated under the head scheme. The allocations under scheme head
are very modest compared to the task entrusted with the Ministry. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the Ministry should device innovative schemes/programmes aimed at improving
HR potential and productivity and seek allocations for them in order to improve quality and
standards of personnel working under the Government. The organizations under the Department
of Personnel and Training play very important role in their respective fields of Governance. The
Committee also recommends that these organizations should also frame Schemes/programmes
aimed at bringing improvements in their systems, procedures and personnel and seek allocations
for such schemes. (Para 2.51)
On a perusal of Annual Report 2016-17 of the Ministry, the Committee observes that
shortage of IAS officers in this country has been a perennial problem since 1951. But now the
vacancy position has increased to an alarming level. With the present rate of recruitment it will
require decades to fill the existing vacancies. The Committee notes that almost all the key and
strategic positions under the Union as well as the States are being manned by the IAS and
persistent shortage in the IAS officers ultimately affects governance in the country. The Committee
expresses its serious concern over persistent shortage of IAS officers and strongly recommends
that all efforts be made to fill these vacancies. The Committee further notes that the Director,
LBSNAA has informed it that Academy has the capacity to train more than 180 officers, it,
therefore, fails to understand as to why lack of training capacity has been cited as one of the
reasons for not filling the vacancies of IAS officers. The Committee feels lack of training
capacity should not become a reason for non-filling of vacancies of IAS officers and if we are
actually short of capacity in this regard, efforts should be made to enhance our capacity to train
more IAS officers and that should not be a difficult to achieve. (Para 3.4)
46

47
As is seen from the above figures, almost all organizations/institutions under the Ministry
are facing acute staff shortage. These organizations are institutions of national importance and
play crucial role in personnel management and governance of the country. If these organizations
are under staffed, they cannot be expected to impart their responsibilities efficiently. The Committee
observes that vacancies in these organizations are a persistent problem and the DoPT cannot
escape its responsibility of ensuring adequate staffing in these institutions. (Para 3.7)
The Committee expresses its displeasure over the persistent shortage of manpower in
these institutions over last many decades and impresses upon the DoPT to devise a potent
mechanism to ensure filling of all vacancies at the earliest, so that the performance of these
institutions does not suffer. Some institutional mechanism must be put in place to ensure that
staff strength of these organizations always remains adequate and responsibilities is fixed in case
timely action is not taken in filling these vacancies. (Para 3.8)
In its previous report on Demands for Grants for the FY 2016-17, the Committee had
recommended that adequate funds should be made available to the CBI to enable it to implement
its Plan schemes to the ideal stipulation. The Committee observes that during the year 2016-17
CBI has lagged behind in utilizing its fund on its plan schemes. In many schemes, expenditure
has remained below 50% of the outlay. The Committee apprehends that such a low pace of fund
utilization may lead to reduction of funds at RE stage for which CBI itself would be responsible.
(Para 3.15)
The CBI has undertaken schemes with the aim to improve its functioning and to make
it a 21st Century premier investigative agency. To achieve this aim, the Committee feels that
the CBI needs to beef up the pace of the implementation of its proposed schemes and monitor
pace of expenditure to ensure their timely completion. The Ministry in their action taken replies
therefore should explain the reasons for such slow pace of expenditure on plan schemes of the
CBI and measures proposed to be taken so that allotted funds are fully and efficiently utilized
by it in future. (Para 3.16)
The Committee expresses its deep concern on the state-of-affairs relating to the vacancy
position in the CBI. This issue was also highlighted in the previous report of the Committee on
the Demands for Grants for the year 2016-17. The Committee is apprehensive that unless the
substantial improvement in vacancy position is achieved immediately, its adverse impact on
performance of agency would become visible sooner than later. The nation is facing problems on
many fronts like internal security, transnational terrorism, cyber-crimes, corruption and many
others and we cannot afford to have such a premier agency understaffed and struggling with
resource crunch. The Committee expresses its dismay over the existing state-of-affairs in the
C.B.I. To overcome the perennial problem of vacancies in the CBI, the Committee recommends
that the Government may consider making direct recruitment (in some proportion) at Group 'A'
level in the agency through UPSC Civil Services Examination. Government may also consider
making terms of deputation to CBI more attractive so that officers from the State Police Forces,
Central Para Military Forces, Intelligence Bureau, etc. are tempted to join CBI on deputation.
(Para 3.17)

48
The Committee endorses the need for capacity enhancement and skill development of the
CBI and commends the proposal of projects like Centralized Technology Vertical (CTV)- CBI,
setting up of International Centre of Excellence in Investigation (ICEI-CBI) and International
Centre of Excellence in Forensic Science. The Committee recommends that approval and
establishment of these projects may be expedited. (Para 3.18)
The CBI in its submission before the Committee stated that one of the major reasons why
investigators do not come on deputation to CBI is the lack of available housing. The overall
housing satisfaction is very low at pan India level and especially in Delhi where the Head Quarter
is situated. As informed by the Agency itself, even after proposed construction/acquisition of new
quarters the satisfaction level would remain substantially low in future also. Accordingly, the
Committee recommends enhancing significantly the allocation for acquiring land and building
staff quarters of CBI at Delhi and other locations, to bring the satisfaction level upto somewhere
near to the level prescribed by the Ministry of Urban Development. The Committee also expresses
its dissatisfaction over failure of CBI to utilize fully funds earmarked for housing for its personnel
and desires that CBI should ensure that funds allocated for the purpose are fully utilized by it.
(Para 3.19)
CAT has been envisaged to provide cheaper and faster adjudication of employees' grievances
against the Government. This, on other hand, was also to help in reducing the burden of Higher
Courts of the country who were already under tremendous pressure due to their twin problems
of pendency and vacancy. Even after thirty years of its establishment, CAT lacks physical as well
as human infrastructure. Nine Benches are not having their own building and more than 30%
of Members have not been appointed. The Committee in its previous report on Demands for
Grants 2016-17 had also given recommendations for strengthening CAT in terms of infrastructure
and human resource. The Committee once again reiterates that proper infrastructure in terms
of physical as well as human, should be provided to CAT, to achieve the desired level of
performance. Going by the present pace of efforts, the situation is unlikely to improve as is
evident from the fact that there are about 30% vacant positions and only about 12 crores has
been earmarked for infrastructure development. The Committee feels that more concerted
efforts are required to make CAT ef fective and to serve the purpose for which it was established.
(Para 3.25)
The Committee notes from the submission made by CAT that it has a requirement of
additional Benches at four places viz. Jabalpur, Cuttack, Jaipur and Lucknow, as only one
Divisional Bench is sanctioned at these places. Absence of any of the two members viz. Judicial
and Administration hampers the work of the Tribunal. There have been PILs filed in the
concerned High Courts at these places where a Bench could not be made functional for want of
either of Members due to various reasons. The Committee is of the view that if need for
additional Bench exists at these places, these need to be set up early so that Central Government
employees get quick justice at these places. (Para 3.26)

49
The Committee has been informed that about 41,849 cases (as on 31/01/2017) are pending
before various benches of CAT. Out of which about 3,823 are pending for more than five years
and about 10,007 are pending for 3-5 years. This is a substantial number. The Committee feels
that it is imperative upon the CAT to make concerted efforts so as to reduce the pendency
substantially. In addition, the Government should also make sustained efforts to streamline the
service rules so that there is minimum litigation; the internal grievance redressal mechanism
within the respective Departments needs to be made more robust to command the faith of the
employees; and a mechanism be evolved so that many of the cases in service matters can be
settled within the system itself so that minimal number of cases go to Tribunal. (Para 3.27)
The Committee recommends that building of NCGC should be constructed at an early date
and necessary infrastructure created for the Centre to perform its activities in an efficient
manner. The Government should also evolve a mechanism to ensure that Centre evolves into
a result oriented organization of global excellence which is self-sustaining and does not remain
dependent on Government funds. (Para 3.34)
As previously discussed in the report (Para 3.6 & 3.7) the Committee is constrained to
refer to the submissions made by the various organizations/institutions within the jurisdiction of
the DoPT, such as, the CBI, CIC, CVC, LBSNAA, ISTM, etc. pointing to the existence of a large
number of vacancies having remained unfilled in those organizations for a number of years and
observes that if large number of the vacancies in the organizations under the Department of
Personnel and Training itself are remaining unfilled for a number of years, the situation in other
organizations of the Government of India would be worse. The Committee, therefore, feels that
the DoPT should in consultation with the recruiting agencies like UPSC and SSC, evolve a
mechanism for timely filling of vacancies in all organizations of the Government. (Para 3.38)
The Committee also recommends that the recruiting agencies like UPSC, SSC should
shorten their recruitment process to the extent possible so that the time between requisition of
vacancies and sending of recommendations of the recruitment agency is reduced to the minimal
possible time. This would ensure that even the recruitment against the vacancies which are not
anticipated in advance is also not delayed unduly. (Para 3.39)
The Staff Selection Commission (SSC) is mandated for recruitment of Group B and C
employees of Government of India, who forms bulk of its strength. In the year 2016-17 the
Commission has examined more than 2.3 crores candidate (for about 70,000 posts) which is
phenomenal in terms of numbers. The Commission has informed that it recently conducted one
of its largest examinations i.e. the Combined Higher Secondary Level Examination (Tier-I), 2016
for approximately 65 Lakhs candidates flawlessly, without any glitch or untoward incident. This
has become possible by shifting of the examination mode from OMR based to computer based.
The Committee appreciates shift to computer-based examinations by the Commission.
(Para 3.46)
The Secretary, DoPT and the Chairman, SSC in their deposition before the Committee
have informed that with the shift to Computer Based examination the cost of conducting

50
examination per candidate has gone up from ````` 100 per candidate to ````` 200 per candidate and
````` 135 crore liability of examinations conducted during FY 2016-17 would be booked during the
financial year 2017-18. Thus, the Commission would be requiring about 251 crore additional
funds during the financial year 2017-18, as the present allocation Professional Services is
inadequate. The Committee therefore, recommends that SSC be provided with the required
additional funds in the financial year 2017-18 at RE stage, so that its work doesn't suffer due
to lack of funds. (Para 3.47)
As Examinations have gone online, the Committee recommends that the SSC must ensure
that software, hardware and other facilities at examination venues are audited and made to
conforms to global standards. Also, problems like server crashing, computer hanging, login
failure, abrupt shutting down of computers during examinations which are real time problems,
being faced in a computer based examination should be adequately taken care of so that no
candidate suffer because of this. (Para 3.48)
The CIC was established in the year 2005 and even after a decade of its establishment,
the CIC is severely understaffed. As per the information provided by the Commission, against
a sanctioned strength of 160 only 25 personnel are on permanent basis and rest are working on
ad-hoc basis. Even after Recruitment Rules are framed the appointments have not been made.
The Committee expresses its dismay over manning of the Commission's Secretariat through ad-
hoc and temporary appointments and strongly recommends that appointments of regular employees
are done at the earliest, so that Commission's working is made more responsive and accountable.
(Para 3.54)
The Committee in its previous report on Demands for Grants 2016-17 has highlighted the
problem of shortage of faculty positions in the Academy and recommended that other feasible
options of handling this problem may be explored. However, no progress is visible in this respect
and the Committee expresses its anguish over it. The Committee again recommends that the
DoPT should explore all possible options for augmenting and expanding its existing training
capacity at the LBSNAA and ISTM and ensure availability of full strength of faculty and other
supporting staff for efficient functioning of these training Institutes. (Para 3.61)
The Committee also observes that the Academy has been slow on spending on scheme/plan
side in the FY 2016-17. Out of ````` 13.70 crore allocated under Capital head, only ````` 9.21 crore have
been spent and out of 14 crore allotted under Revenue head only 8.74 crore have been spent.
In view of under-utilization of fund sought on scheme/plan side, the Committee observes that
every spending unit should make a prudent assessment of its requirement of funds under plan
schemes it proposes to undertake and seek of budgetary allocations to the extent it can utilize.
Non-utilisation of allocated funds put unnecessary financial burden on the Government and,
therefore, it should be avoided. Also, strategies should be drawn for the utilization of full funds
made available to spending units and utilization should be closely monitored to ensure efficient
utilization of funds. (Para 3.62)

51
IIPA is a premier institution on Public Administration in India under the patronship of the
Hon'ble Vice-President of India. The Committee is pained to observe that such an institution of
national importance is not able to raise adequate funds for its maintenance and performance of
its functions. Institutions like IIPA needs to be protected, nurtured and nourished, but side by
side such premier Institution should become self-sustaining and should be able to raise themselves
the resources needed by them and not depend on public funds. The Committee recommends that
Government should render all possible help to this Institute to make it a self-sustaining Institute
of global excellence and for that if public funds are to be provided for some time, it should be
done. (Para 3.68)
Dealing with the grievances of citizen effectively is one of the core components of Good
Governance. CPGRAMS is a good initiative of the Government for redressal of citizen grievances.
However, public at large, particularly those who are living in rural and far-flung areas needs to
be made aware of existence of such grievance redressal system. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that this system of Public Grievance Redressal (CPGRAMS) should be publicized in
mass media in vernacular languages, so that common people become aware of availability of such
avenue for redressal of their grievances against the Government organisations. (Para 3.76)
The Committee feels that the spirit of Public Grievances Redressal Mechanism is primarily
to resolve the grievances in a professional and satisfactory manner. The relief and remedial
mechanism need to fix the accountability on the decision making authorities. As in the event of
unsatisfactory redressal of their grievances, the public usually approach courts for redressal of
their grievances which increases burden of courts, every endeavour should be made that grievances
are resolved in a professional and satisfactory manner. (Para 3.77)
In order to make grievance redressal system (CPGRAMS) more effective, it is recommended
that Government may also consider making a provision for appeal in the existing system.
(Para 3.78)
The Committee also takes note of the fact that over the time there has been a substantial
increase in the number of public grievances received by the Department. The Committee desires
that all those areas where large number of grievances are received, are examined and in those
common areas of grievances, after analyzing the root cause, systemic changes should be brought
in to reduce the volume of grievances pertaining to them. Also, suo-motu information relating
to those areas should be largely publicized on the Department's website, news papers and other
such media. (Para 3.79)
Further, as of now, 21 States/UTs have enacted statute for time bound delivery of services.
The Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redress of their
Grievances Bill, 2011 was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 20th December, 2011. However, it could
not be passed and lapsed with the dissolution of the 15th Lok Sabha. The Committee feels that
Delivery of Government Services and Grievance Redressal should have statutory backing. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should consider re-introduction of the
said Bill in the year 2017-18. (Para 3.80)

CHAPTER-I
BRIEF OVERVIEW OF THE MINISTRY
1.0 The Ministry of Law and Justice owes its origin to the Charter Act, 1833 enacted by British
Parliament. In accordance with the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the
Ministry comprises three Departments, namely, Department of Legal Affairs, Legislative Department and
Department of Justice. The key mandate of the Ministry is to provide policy support in administration
of Justice; furnishing of legal advice to Government of India and defend Government of India in various
Courts and Tribunals and draft supreme and subordinate legislations for Government of India, etc.
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
1.1 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, the Department of Legal
Affairs renders advice to various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal matters and
carries out the litigation work in various Courts and Tribunals. Besides this, it is also concerned with
the appointment of Law Officers, namely, the Attorney General of India, the Solicitor General of India
and the Additional Solicitor Generals of India; assists in entering into treaties with foreign countries in
matters of civil law on behalf of the President of India. It is also the nodal authority in respect of
Appellate Tribunal for Foreign Exchange, Income Tax Appellate Tribunal and National Tax Tribunal. The
Department of Legal Affairs has a two-tier set-up, namely, the Main Secretariat at New Delhi and the
Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Banglore.
1.2 Following Institutions/organizations are under the overall supervision of Department of Legal
Affairs:-
(a) Law Commission of India:-  The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body,
constituted by the Government once in three years. It consists of a Chairman, three full-
time Members, one Member-Secretary and three or more part-time Members, depending
upon the nature of work. The Twenty-first Law Commission headed by Dr. Justice Balbir
Singh Chauhan was constituted with effect from 1st September, 2015 for a three year term
ending on 31st August, 2018.
(b) Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT):- ITAT is one of the oldest Tribunals, setup under
Section 252 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 to hear appeals against order passed by authorities
mentioned under Section 253 of IT Act. It has 63 Benches covering all cities having seat
of High Courts.
(c) Appellate Tribunal of Foreign Exchange (ATFE): - The Appellate Tribunal of Foreign
Exchange was established on 1st June, 2000 vide Government of India Notification No.
S.O. 531 (E), dated 1.6.2000 issued under Section 18 of the Foreign Exchange Management
Act, 1999 (FEMA).

2
(d) Bar Council of India (BCI):-  The Bar Council of India is a statutory body constituted
under section 4 of the Advocates Act, 1961, which has been empowered among other
things to lay down standards of professional conduct and etiquette for lawyers, regulate the
standard of legal practice and legal education in the country.
(e) International Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution (ICADR):-  The International
Centre for Alternate Dispute Resolution was registered under the Societies Registration Act,
1860 on 31st May 1995. It is an autonomous organisation working under the aegis of the
Department.
(f) Indian Law Institute (ILI):- The Indian Law Institute registered under the Societies
Registration Act, 1860, is engaged in research in the field of law. It was inaugurated on 12th
December, 1959 by Dr. Rajendra Prasad, the then President of India. The Institute has been
granted Deemed University status in 2004.
LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT
1.3 The Legislative Department acts mainly as a service provider in so far as the legislative business
of the Union Government is concerned. The Department is entrusted with legislative matters and is
responsible for drafting of all Government Bills and Ordinances and scrutiny and vetting of Subordinate
legislations sponsored by various Union Ministries/Departments. Rendering assistance to Parliament and
Joint/Standing/Select Committees in respect to Bills before its enactment. It is also administratively
concerned with certain matters i.e. the Code of Civil Procedure, Limitation, Arbitration, Contracts,
Personal Laws, Evidence and Transfer of Property.
1.4 The Department has following two wings under it:-
(i) Official Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan: The Official Languages Wing
is a successor organisation to the Official Languages (Legislative) Commission under the
Legislative Department. It has been entrusted with the preparation and publication of a
standard legal terminology for use in all Official Languages; authoritative texts in Hindi of
all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the President, all Rules,
Regulations and Orders made by the Central Government under any Central Act and
authoritative texts of all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the
President in the respective Official Languages of the States and to arrange for the translation
of all Acts passed and Ordinances promulgated in any State into Hindi, if the texts of such
Acts or Ordinances are in a language other than Hindi.
(ii) Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan: The Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan is mainly concerned with bringing
out authoritative Hindi versions of reportable judgements of the Supreme Court and the High
Courts with the objective of promoting the progressive use of Hindi in the legal field. It
brings out various publications of legal literature in Hindi and also holds exhibitions in
various States for giving wide publicity to legal literatures available in Hindi and to promote
their sales.

3
1.5 Election Commission of India: Election Commission of India is an autonomous constitutional
authority created under Article 324 of Constitution for superintendence, direction, control of elections to
Parliament, State legislature, and to offices of the President and the Vice-President of India. The Election
Commission of India is a multi-member body (since 1993) headed by the Chief Election Commissioner
who acts as Chairman of the Commission. The Commission is assisted by Deputy Election Commissioners,
Chief Electoral Officers (CEO), District Election Officers (DEO) and Electoral Registration Officers
(ERO) appointed by the Election Commission under Representation of People Act, 1951. It recognizes/
derecognizes political parties and allot symbols to them. It also implements Model Code of Conduct
(MCC) for smooth conduct of free and fair election. An exclusive demand (Demand No. 62) under which
Budgetary allocation is sought for running activities of Election Commission of India.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
1.6 The duties of the Department of Justice, as per the Government of India (Allocation of Business)
Rules, 1961, include the administration of justice and the processing of appointment of judges of the
Supreme Court and High Courts, appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial Officers in Union
Territories, creation of All India Judicial Service and extension/exclusion of the jurisdiction of a High
Court to a Union Territory.
1.7 The following institutions/autonomous bodies/policy initiatives come under the administrative control
of the Department:
(a) Supreme Court of India:- The Supreme Court of India is the highest constitutional court
and also the final court of appeal.
(b) National Legal Services Authority (NALSA):- The National Legal Services Authority has
been constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to provide legal-aid to the
poor and marginalized sections of society. The Chief Justice of India (CJI) is the patron-
in-chief and second senior most judge of Supreme Court is the Executive Chairman of the
authority. Besides providing free legal aid, it organizes Lok Adalats, off and on, for amicable
settlement of disputes. The NALSA issues guidelines for the State Legal Services Authorities
to implement the legal-aid programmes which are in turn discharged through the following
services:-
(i) Free Legal Services : It includes court fees, process fee and all charges payable or
incurred in connection with any legal proceedings, providing Advocate in legal
proceedings, etc.
(ii) Lok Adalats : Lok Adalat is one of the Alternative Disputes Resolution Mechanisms.
It is a forum where the disputes/cases pending in the court of law or at pre-litigation
stage are settled/compromised amicably. The Lok Adalat has been given statutory
status under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. Under this Act, an award made
by a Lok Adalat is deemed to be a decree of a civil court and is final and binding
on all parties and no appeal lies against thereto before any court.

4
(c) Family Courts/Special Courts :- The Family Court Act, 1984 was enacted with a view
to providing for establishment of Family Courts, to promote conciliation and secure speedy
settlement of disputes relating to marriage, family affairs and related matters. In accordance
with the provisions of Section 3 of the Act, the State/UT Governments can establish Family
Courts in the areas comprising districts, towns, cities in the States having population of ten
lakhs. Even the States/UTs are competent to establish such court in those areas with the
State/UT having a population less than ten lakhs in consultation with the concerned High
Court.
(d) National Judicial Academy:- The National Judicial Academy was registered as a society
under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 and came into existence with effect from 17th
August, 1993. The affairs of the Academy are managed by a Governing Council, which is
chaired by the Chief Justice of India. The registered office of the Academy is in Supreme
Court Building at New Delhi and another office was established in August, 2000 at Bhopal.
The main objectives of the Academy are to impart training to the Judicial Officers of the
States/Union Territories and to study the court management and administration of justice in
States and Union territories.
(e) Centrally Sponsored Scheme: The government is implementing a Centrally Sponsored
Scheme (CSS) for development of infrastructure facilities for judiciary since 1993-94. The
scheme covers construction of court buildings and residential accommodation of judicial
officers/judges covering only Subordinate courts. Under the Scheme, funds are provided to
the States to augment their capacities for infrastructure development of the District and
Subordinate Courts.
(f) National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms: Set up for five years in 2011,
and became fully functional with effect from the financial year 2012-13. The twin goals of
the Mission include increasing access by reducing delays and arrears in the system and
enhancing accountability at all levels through structural changes and setting performance
standards and facilitating enhancement of capacities for achieving such performance standards.
The two schemes proposed to be pursued under the Mission are as under:
(i) Action Research and Judicial Reforms
(ii) Access to Justice- Government of India Project.
(g) Access to Justice- Externally Aided Project (UNDP assisted)  The Project started in 2009
with support under the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The Project is
being implemented in seven States (Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha,
Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh) and aims to strengthen access to justice for the marginalized
- particularly women, scheduled castes, scheduled tribes and minorities - by supporting
strategies and initiatives that seek to address the barriers they face. The duration of the
project is from January, 2013- December, 2017.

5
(h) Computerization of District and Subordinate Courts
E-courts Mission Mode Project Phase-I & II:- This is a scheme proposed in the Twelfth
Plan with components such as computerisation of 1000 new Courts, use of solar energy
under e-Courts Project, computerisation of the Public Prosecutors Office, video-conferencing
facility for jails, enhancement of ICT infrastructure of courts, digitization of old case
records, computerisation of Judicial libraries, up-gradation of application software, SMS
based services, Touch Screen Kiosks with a provision of ` 1280 crore which would spread
over a period of five years.
(i) Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008:- The Gram
Nyayalayas Act, 2008 has been enacted by the Parliament to provide for the establishment
of the Gram Nyayalayas at the grass root level for the purpose of providing speedy and
inexpensive access to justice to the citizens at their door steps. The Central Government
would meet 50 percent of the recurring expenses to be incurred on the setting up of these
courts in the first three years subject to a ceiling of ` 3.20 lakhs per annum.
(j) The Fourteenth Finance Commission has recommended ` 9,749 crore to the Department
of Justice for pendency reduction by establishing additional courts, Fast Track Courts,
establishment of Family Courts, redesigning existing courts to make them litigant-friendly,
augmenting technical support for e-courts, scanning and digitalization, enhancing access to
justice- Legal-aid, Lok Adalats, Alternative Dispute Resolution, Training and capacity building
of judges, public prosecutors, mediators and lawyers and establishing State Judicial Academies
for Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura.

6
CHAPTER-II
AN OVERVIEW OF THE BUDGET ALLOCATIONS DURING 2017-18
2.0 The total proposed budgetary allocations for the Ministry of Law and Justice for the year
2017-18 are shown under the following three Demands:-
(i) Demand No. 61 is the consolidated Budget Estimates pertaining to the Department of Legal
Affairs, the Legislative Department and the Department of Justice under the Ministry of
Law and Justice;
(ii) Demand No. 62 pertains to the Election Commission, which is under the administrative
control of the Legislative Department; and
(iii) Demand No. 63 pertains to the Supreme Court of India, which is under the administrative

SYSTEMATIC VOTERS EDUCATION AND ELECTORAL PARTICIPATION (SVEEP)
4.5 The Commission has taken up a Systematic Voters Education and Electoral Participation (SVEEP)

initiatives should not be crippled for want of adequate funds and recommends that adequate

4.7 The EVMs are procured from Central Public Sector Undertakings, BEL and ECIL. The BEL has
its unit in Bengaluru and ECIL has its unit in Hyderabad. Ballot unit plus control unit together cost

EVM is imported and is tamper-proof. EVM and VVPAT are under the custody of Election Commission
of India but tendring and budgetary provisions are routed though Legislative Department.
4.8 V oter-Verified Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) is a method of providing feedback to voters using a ballot
less voting system. Under VVPAT, a printer-like apparatus is linked to Electronic V oting Machine (EVM).
When a vote is cast, a receipt is generated showing the serial number, name and symbol of the candidate.
It confirms the vote and the voter can verify the details.

4.15 According to Census 2011 and National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), migrants
constitute about 30 per cent of the country's population and also of the total working force. The
Economic Survey (2016-17) also noted that annual migration in the country increased to 9.00
million in 2016 from 3.30 million in 2011. As per the existing law they can cast their vote in the
constituencies where they are registered as voters. During the elections they are not able to cast
their vote at their place of work or in their constituency as they are constantly on move from
one place to another in search of better livelihood. The Commission during the Demands for
Grants (2017-18) informed that a Committee was constituted to look into the issues of domestic
migrant and it has already given its recommendations, which has been forwarded to Legislative
Department, to enable them to cast their vote at their place of work or business. The Committee,
accordingly, recommends the Commission and the Legislative Department to expedite the matter
so that domestic migrants are not deprived of their right to vote which is a basic right of every
citizen in the country.

COMMON ELECTORAL ROLL
4.19 It has been observed that in many cases, a particular elector is registered as a voter at multiple
places, which is a cause of concern and worry. It gives rise to electoral mal-practices, including bogus
voting. The Commission during the meeting submitted that the Election Commission has data for the
entire country and the central server of the Commission is with C-DAC, Pune. The State Election
Commissions are independent bodies and have their own electoral rolls. Some of them prepare their own
electoral rolls and some use electoral rolls of Election Commission of India. The Commission further
submitted that with the help of software the Commission is able to detect a large number of bogus voters
in the country. In the case of recent Assembly election in the States of Uttar Pradesh (32 lakh),
Uttarakhand (42 Thousand), Goa (15 Thousand) and Punjab (2.37 lakh) bogus voters were removed
from the electoral rolls.
4.20 The Committee is happy to know that digitization of electoral rolls and use of software has
helped the Commission to detect a large number of bogus voters in the electoral rolls. This is
a welcome step towards purification of electoral rolls in the country. The Committee is of the
view that linking voter with the Aadhar Card number may further help prevent bogus voters
from enrolling in the electoral rolls. The Committee, though is aware that Election Commission
of India and State Election Commissions are independent bodies, yet an initiative should be
taken to prepare common digital electoral roll which could be used both by Election Commission

21
of India and State Election Commissions. This would not only save huge national resources but
would also be a major step forward towards purification of electoral rolls.
REGISTRATION/DE-REGISTRATION OF POLITICAL PARTIES
4.21 Ours is a multi-party democracy. As per statistics made available to the Committee, there are 7
National Parties, 48 State parties and 1864 registered parties (but not recognized) as on 22nd February,
2017. Political parties are registered with Election Commission in terms of Section 29A of The Representation
of the People Act, 1951. Under Clause 6(A) and 6(B) of the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment)
Order, 1968, parties are recognized as National and State Parties on the basis of their poll performance
at General Elections. Those parties which do not fulfill the requirements of 6A and 6B of the Act in the
next General Election still continue to retain with recognition for one more General Election to the House.
If that party fails to come up with the required level of poll performance in second General Election,
the recognition of that party is withdrawn at that stage. Besides that the Election Commission is
empowered to suspend or withdraw recognition of a party or its failure to observe model code of
conduct. Recognised/Registered political parties are entitled to certain benefit which are enumerated
below:
Registered Un-recognized
(i) The candidates set up by a political party registered with the Election Commission of India
will get preference in the matter of allotment of free symbols vis-a-vis independent candidates.
(ii) Registered political parties, in course of time, can get recognition as 'State Party' or 'National
Party' subject to the fulfillment of the conditions prescribed by the Commission in the
Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, as amended from time to time.
(iii) As per Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the registered political
parties are entitled to get the benefit of exemption on the expenses incurred on travel
expenses in connection with campaigning by their leaders (not exceeding twenty in number).
(iv) As per para 10B of the Election Symbol (Reservation 86 Allotment) Order, 1968, as one time
facility, the candidates of registered political parties are entitled for the concession of
common symbol in a general election(s) to the Legislative Assembly or House of the people,
subject to the fulfillment of the conditions prescribed by the Commission in the aforesaid
Symbol Order, 1968.
(v) As per the provisions of Section 29C of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the
political parties have to submit a report of contributions received in excess of ` 20,000/-
before the due date for furnishing a return of its income of that financial year under section
139 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, (43 of 1961) to the Commission. The said report is sent
to Central Board of Direct Taxes for tax relief under that Act.
Registered Recognised
(i) The Election Symbols are reserved for these parties to contest elections as per the provisions
of the above mentioned Order.

22
(ii) As per Section 77 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the recognized political
parties are entitled with campaigning by their leaders (not exceeding forty in number).
(iii) Two copies of the electoral roll, one printed copy and another in CD are supplied to
recognized political parties, free of cost, after draft and final publications under the provisions
of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960.
(iv) Under Rule 85 D of the Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961, the candidates of recognized
parties are provided one copy of the electoral roll used for conduct of general election free
of cost.
(v) Facilities of broadcasts on Akashvani and Doordarshan are given to recognized political
parties (Compendium of Instructions on Conduct of Elections - V olume II/Inst. S. No. 47)
4.22 As to deregistration of political parties, the Committee has been apprised that the Commission has
not been vested with the powers to deregister political parties. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in its
judgement in the case of Indian National Congress (I) vs. Institute of Social Welfare and Others
(Appeal(civil) 3320-21 of 2001), [(2002) 5 SCC 685] has observed that the Election Commission can
cancel registration of political parties under the following three situations only:-
• where a political party has obtained registration by practicing fraud or forgery;
• where a registered political party amends its nomenclature of association, rules and regulations
abrogating therein conforming to the provisions of Section 29A (5) of the Act or intimating
the Election Commission that it has ceased to have faith and allegiance to the Constitution
of India or to the principles of socialism, secularism and democracy or it would not uphold
the sovereignty, unity and integrity of india so as to comply with the provisions of Section
29A(5) of the Act; and
• Any like ground where no enquiry is called for on that part of the Commission.

NOTARIES APPOINTMENT
5.21 The administration of the Notaries Act, 1952 and the Notaries Rules, 1956 are within the purview
of the Notary Cell of the Department of Legal Affairs. The Schedule under Rule 8(4A) of the Notaries
Rules, 1956, Central Government has fixed the quota of maximum number of Notaries to be appointed
by the Central Government as well as maximum number of Notaries to be appointed by State/UT
Government. Central Government enhances the quota allotted to State Governments on receipt of request
for the purpose from the State Government concerned.
5.22 In its written replies to the questionnaire on the appointment of Notaries, the Department of Legal
Affairs submitted that according to Rule 3, of the Notaries Act, 1952, any advocate who had been
practicing for ten years is eligible for appointment as Notary except for women and person belonging
to SC/ST/OBC category. Rule 4 to 8 of the Notaries Rules prescribe the procedure for appointment of
Notaries. These rules stipulate that applicant will be called for an interview and only upon recommendation
of the interview board an applicant shall be appointed as Notary. However, the Notaries Rules, 1956 do
not provide for any time-limit for these appointments. The interviews are being held on the discretion
of the appropriate Government and the decision for interview of applicants from a particular State is
taken after assessing the demand i.e. number of applications received for appointment in that particular
State. The notaries appointed by such procedure are being issued a Certificate of Practice which remains
valid for a period of five years. As regards renewal procedure of Notary, it may be mentioned that Rule
8B of the Notaries Rules provides for renewal of Certificate of practice. It stipulates that any application
for renewal of certificate of practice shall be submitted before six months of its expiry. However,
Government may after considering the reasons stated in the application, relax the condition of submission
of application for renewal of certificate of practice before the specified period.
5.23 The Committee is of the view that Notaries are important link in the judicial system and
provide cost effective services to public for various basic services viz., verification, authentication,
certification of documents etc. in the country. The Committee is of the opinion that the process
of appointment of Notaries needs to be further streamlined and made more robust so that
competent persons are appointed as Notaries.

6.16 The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, cast duty upon the court to supply certain documents
including chargesheet, First Information Report, statements of witnesses, confessions and other
documents of investigation on which the prosecution proposes to rely without delay to the
accused free of cost. In reality, these documents are supplied to the accused by the prosecution/
police who is also a party to the dispute. Referring to Sections 207 and 208 of Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973, the Committee observes that the court instead of discharging its duty to supply
requisite documents (except voluminous one) which is essential for free and fair trial has been
largely passing the buck to Police. The Apex Court, time and again, particularly, in the case of
Shri Jahid Shaikh v. State of Gujarat (2011) 7 SCC 762 has held that when many of the accused
persons were not provided with copies of the chargesheet and the other relevant documents as
indicated in Sections 207 and 208 of CrPC, it seriously affects the right of an accused to a free
and fair trial. The Committee understands that in addition to safeguarding rights and interest
of the victim, it is also a solemn duty of the court to provide requisite documents to the accused.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Department of Justice should take necessary steps
to ensure full and proper compliance of the aforesaid provisions of Code of Criminal Procedure,
1973.

COMPUTERISATION OF DISTRICT AND SUBORDINATE COURTS
1. e-Courts Mission Mode Project Phase-I
6.23 The e-Courts Integrated Mission Mode Project is one of the National eGovernance projects
(NeGP), with the objective to provide designated services to litigants, lawyers and the judiciary. The
project facilitates automation of case management workflow through use of application software for
activities such as Case Filing, Scrutiny, Registration, Case Allocation, Court Proceedings, Details entry
of a Case, Case Disposal and restoration, Transfer of Case, Pendency data / Institution Registers, Court
Diaries, Calculation of court fees etc. The national e-Courts portal (http://www.ecourts.gov.in) provides

38
online services to litigants such as details of case registration, cause list, case status, daily orders, and
final judgments. Litigants and lawyers are also provided services through Judicial Service Centre at the
court complexes such as Case Filing, Certified copies of orders and judgments, Case status etc. The
Department in its written submission stated that sites for all at the end of Phase-I of the project in 2015,
of the total target of 14,249 District and Subordinate courts to be computerized, sites for all 14,249
courts (100 percent) have been made ready for computerisation, out of which LAN has been installed
at 13,643 courts (95.75 per cent), hardware at 13,436 courts (94.3 per cent) and software at 13,672
courts (96 per cent).
(II) e-Courts Mission Mode Project Phase-II
6.24 This Scheme is built upon the experience of the e-Courts Project Phase - I. In Phase-II the
Department has planned to give various types of computer material to 5,751 courts, and the ones which

• A new revamped eCourts portal with improved citizen interface. The portal has recorded
more than 41.78 Crore transactions during Ph-II of the project.
• eCourts portal provides status of 7 crores pending and disposed cases and more than 3
crore orders/ judgments pertaining to more than 16,000 courts.
• National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG) has been opened to public in Sept, 2015.
• A new, more user friendly version of Case Information Software (NC 2.0) has been
developed and all computerised courts are being migrated to it. The eCommittee is also
working towards integrating High Courts and Supreme Court data into this software.
• Video Conferencing facility has been operationalised between 500 courts and corresponding
prisons.
• During Ph-II, 6.66 Cr SMSs auto-generated through the system have been sent to the

• Nineteen states/UT's have signed and executed the tripartite MoU's till 31st December, 2016

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS — AT A GLANCE
The Committee observes that the projection under BE (2016-17) of the Ministry was
reduced at RE stage. This implies that either spending units have over estimated their expenditure
or the utilization pace was tardy. Either of the two situations is not desirable as unutilized funds
mean unnecessary financial burden on the Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that every unit of the Ministry should realistically assess its requirement of funds and seek
funds only on the basis of its realistic requirements andclosely monitor expenditure so that
situation of large amount of funds remaining unutilized is avoided. The Committee recommends
units which are not able to utilize funds sought by them should be made accountable for it.
(Para 2.9)
The Committee expresses its displeasure over non-utilisation of funds allocated to Official
Languages Wing and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan year after year despite Committee's repeated
recommendations of full utilization of funds allotted. The Committee is also not happy with the
reasons furnished for non-utilisation of funds. Matter ought to have been taken up with the
Government of India Press if delayed receipt of its bills was contributing to non-utilisation of
funds. As regards other reasons, the units ought to have asked for lower funds if it was to reduce
its expenditure on account of economy instructions. The Committee would expect units to project
their requirements realistically and thereafter closely monitor spending of allocated funds to
avoid under-utilisation of funds. (Para 3.6)
The Committee observes that the Institute has been in existence for almost 3 decades now
and substantial amount of public fund already spent on it. It would, therefore, be useful for the
Department to get a third party evaluation made of the quality of training being imparted at the
Institute and the extent to which training at the Institute has resulted in improved legislative
drafting skills, so that shortcomings, if any, could be removed and Institute evolves into a
globally reputed centre for legislative drafting. (Para 3.9)
The Committee observes that as against the projection of Rs.283.51 crore, only Rs.146
crore have been allocated in BE (2017-18), which is a short fall of 46 per cent (approx.), with
major reductions being under the head office expenses and voters awareness. The Committee is
of the view that voters awareness is crucial for strengthening of democracy and adequate funds
should be provided to the Commission for it. The Committee recommends that, if needed,
allocations for it should be enhanced suitably at RE stage so that campaign for voters awareness
is not impacted adversely for want of funds. (Para 4.4)
The Committee appreciates the activities undertaken by ECI and is of the view that
programmes like Systematic Voters Education and Electoral Participation (SVEEP) are very
important in increasing voters turn-out. The Committee is of the view that such important
initiatives should not be crippled for want of adequate funds and recommends that adequate
funds for these programmes should be made available to the Commission. (Para 4.6)
